title: Troubleshooting
text: Some R packages have to be compiled when you install them. If install.packages() fails with errors about compilers, make, gfortran, or missing files like cmath, follow the steps for your computer below.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Windows users – installing Rtools (required for compiling R packages)
text:
Windows users – installing Rtools (required for compiling R packages)
Some R packages are available only as source code. On Windows you need Rtools (a collection of compilers and build utilities) so that R can install those packages. macOS and Linux already ship suitable build tools; Windows does not.

Do I already have Rtools?

In a fresh R session (the Positron Console) run:
Sys.which("make")

If you get a blank result (““), R cannot find make ⇒ Rtools is missing. • If you see a full path containing rtools….exe, you’re all set! NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!


Find the Rtools version that matches your R

Check your R version:
R.version.string

Your R version Install this Rtools 4.5.x Rtools45 4.4.x Rtools44 4.3.x Rtools43 4.2.x Rtools42 (no longer needed if you upgraded R)


Download Rtools


Go to https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/ Click the folder for your version (e.g. rtools43 for 4.3; rtools44 for 4.4; rtools45 for 4.5). Download the .exe installer (≈ 200 MB).


Install Rtools


Close Positron (or RStudio). Run the downloaded installer. When prompted, tick “Add Rtools to system PATH.” Accept the default install path (C:, C:, …). Finish the installation (it may take a minute).


Verify the installation


After installation open a new R session (or reboot) and run:

Sys.which("make")
#>                  make 
#> "C:\\rtools45\\usr\\bin\\make.exe"   # or rtools44 / rtools43

title: Troubleshooting
section: Mac users – installing gfortran and Xcode Command Line Tools (required for compiling R packages)
text:
Mac users – installing gfortran and Xcode Command Line Tools (required for compiling R packages)

macOS users – installing gfortran (required for compiling R packages)
Some R packages require a Fortran compiler to install from source.
macOS does not include one by default.
You need to install gfortran manually and the version must match your R version.


Do I already have gfortran?

In a fresh R session (the Positron Console) run:
Sys.which("gfortran") 

If you get a blank result (““), gfortran is missing ⇒ you need to install it.
If you see a path like /opt/gfortran/bin/gfortran, you’re all set! NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!


Find the gfortran version that matches your R Check your R version:


Look at the top of the R console window OR
copy/paste this into your terminal

R.version.string 

If your R version is 4.5.x Install gfortran
If your R version is 4.3 to 4.4.x install gfortran 12.2
If you R version is older then no need to install gfortran


Download gfortran


https://mac.r-project.org/tools/gfortran-12.2-universal.pkg
https://mac.r-project.org/tools/gfortran-14.2-universal.pkg


Install gfortran


Close Positron (or RStudio).
Double-click the downloaded .pkg file.
Follow the installer prompts and accept the default install path. Enter your Mac password when prompted. Finish the installation.


Verify the installation After installation open a new R session and run:

Sys.which("gfortran") 
#\> gfortran 
#\> "/opt/gfortran/bin/gfortran" 

If you see the path above, gfortran is installed correctly ✅
If you still get a blank result, try restarting your Mac and running again.


One more check - verify R and gfortran are in sync


Run this in R:

system("gfortran --version") 
You should see output like:
GNU Fortran (GCC) 14.2.0 # if you are on R 4.5 
GNU Fortran (GCC) 12.2.0 # if you are on R 4.4 or 4.3 

If the version number does not match your R version, you have the wrong gfortran installed and need to download the correct version from https://mac.r-project.org/tools/
macOS users – fixing missing C++ header files (required for compiling R packages)

If you see errors like these when installing packages:
fatal error: 'cmath' file not found 
fatal error: 'cstdlib' file not 
found fatal error: 'cstring' file not found 
This means your Xcode Command Line Tools are missing or out of date. This is common after a macOS upgrade.

Do I have this problem?

In R run:
system("xcode-select -p")

If you get an error or a blank result ⇒ Command Line Tools are missing. • If you see /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools ⇒ they are installed. NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!


Fix the problem Close Positron (or RStudio) completely. Open the Mac Terminal application and run these commands one at a time:


Step 1 - Remove the old Command Line Tools:
sudo rm -rf /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools 

You will be prompted for your Mac password.
Type it and press Enter (you will not see the password as you type - this is normal).



Step 2 - Reinstall the Command Line Tools:
xcode-select --install 

A popup window will appear.
Click Install and wait for it to finish.
This may take 5 to 10 minutes depending on your internet connection



Step 3 - Verify the installation was successful:
xcode-select -p 

You should see:

/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools

Try installing your packages again


Once the Command Line Tools are installed, reopen Positron and re-run the install.packages() line in Part 2 of the Session 1 student script.



⚠️ Note for macOS beta users:
If you are running a beta version of macOS, package compilation errors are more likely because R and its tools may not yet be fully compatible with the newest macOS releases. If you continue to have problems after reinstalling the Command Line Tools, the most reliable solution is to use the stable (non-beta) release of macOS.


🔑 Quick Reference Card
Your Setup R Version Need
Windows 4.5.x = Rtools45
Windows 4.4.x = Rtools44
Windows 4.3.x = Rtools43
Mac 4.5.x = gfortran 14.2
Mac 4.4.x or 4.3.x = gfortran 12.2
Mac (any version) = any Xcode Command Line Tools

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
⬇ Student script ⬇ Solutions ⬇ Workshop folder (ZIP)
Where this session fits. Most data projects go through the same steps, whatever the topic. Today covers Visualize and Save and share (highlighted): more kinds of plots, chosen colors, and saving plots to files you can put in a report.
crumbs: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
Order the bars
Alphabetical order rarely helps. fct_infreq() orders by count (most common first), and fct_rev() flips it so the longest bar is at the top:

👀 Follow along 2.2 — Order the bars with fct_rev(fct_infreq(hospital_name)), and add a fill color and labs().


ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(hospital_name)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Cases by hospital", x = "Number of cases", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()














Tip🧩 Reading a function call



Here is the core of the plot you just made, taken apart:
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(hospital_name)))) + geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6")








Piece
What it is
What it does




ggplot(...)
the function that starts every plot
sets up an empty plot


data = linelist
a named argument of ggplot()
the data to plot


mapping = aes(...)
a named argument, filled in by the aes() function
links columns to parts of the plot (“aesthetics”)


y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(hospital_name))
an argument of aes()
puts the hospitals on the y-axis, in the order of their counts


+
the plus sign
adds the next layer to the plot


geom_bar(...)
a function that adds a layer
draws one bar per hospital, counting its rows


fill = "#2a78d6"
an argument of geom_bar(), outside aes()
colors every bar the same blue



Inside the brackets, R works from the inside out: fct_infreq() orders the hospitals by count, then fct_rev() reverses that order. The + signs then build the plot layer by layer, from left to right: first the empty plot, then the bars, then the labels and the theme.








Note🔍 What this code does




fct_infreq(hospital_name) turns the hospital names into categories ordered by how often they appear, most common first.
fct_rev() reverses that order. On a horizontal chart the first category is drawn at the bottom, so reversing it puts the longest bar (Other/Unknown, 2354 cases) at the top.
geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") colors every bar blue. fill is outside aes() here, so it’s one fixed color, not linked to a column.
labs() sets the title and the axis titles. y = NULL removes the y-axis title: the hospital names speak for themselves.
theme_minimal() removes the gray background and keeps light grid lines.
crumbs: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
Fill by a second variable
Map fill to split each bar. The position argument controls how the pieces are arranged:

👀 Follow along 2.3 — x = age_cat, fill = outcome, with position = "stack", "fill", and "dodge" (the next three code blocks).


# "stack" (the default): counts, stacked
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack")









# "fill": every bar is 100% — compares PROPORTIONS across groups
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")









# "dodge": side by side — compares COUNTS within each group
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")














Note🔍 What this code does




fill = outcome is inside aes(), so it’s linked to a column: each bar is split into one colored piece per outcome, and ggplot adds a legend. These are ggplot’s default colors; in Part 4 you choose your own.
position = "stack" piles the pieces on top of each other, so the bar height is the number of cases. Under 18 has 3962 cases and 80+ only 1, so the older groups are hard to see.
position = "fill" stretches every bar to the same height, from 0 to 1 (0% to 100%). You compare proportions: what share of each age group recovered, died, or has an unknown outcome.
position = "dodge" puts the pieces side by side. You compare counts within each group: in most age groups the Death bar is taller than the Recover bar (Under 18: 1755 deaths, 1322 recoveries).









Note🤔 Think about it: which version answers “do older patients die more often?”





The 100% "fill" version. The stacked version mostly shows that there are many more young patients than old ones, so the small bars for older groups are hard to compare.









Important✏️ TRY IT 2 (3 min): cases by district



Make a horizontal bar chart of measles cases by district, longest bar on top.
✅ Check: North is at the top; Unknown is at the bottom






NoteShow solution






ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(district)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Measles cases by district", x = "Number of cases", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()








fct_infreq() puts North (342 cases) first, and fct_rev() moves it to the top. Unknown (34 cases) ends up at the bottom.











Note📖 Good to know




Inside or outside aes()? Inside aes(), a setting is linked to a column and changes from bar to bar (aes(fill = outcome)). Outside, it’s one fixed value for everything (geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6")).
A common mistake is a color name inside aes(): aes(fill = "blue"). ggplot treats “blue” as a category called “blue”, draws it in its first default color (a salmon red), and adds a legend for it.

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
Rotate long labels
If you keep labels on the x-axis, rotate them so they don’t overlap:

ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = hospital_name)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))














Important✏️ TRY IT 4 (4 min): vaccination by age group



Make a 100% bar chart of vaccinated by age_cat, with vacc_colors, a percent y-axis, labels, and theme_minimal().
✅ Check: every bar reaches 100%; “Yes” is blue in every bar






NoteShow solution






ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vacc_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Vaccination status of measles cases by age group",
    x     = "Age group",
    y     = "Percent of cases",
    fill  = "Vaccinated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








position = "fill" makes every bar 100%, and because vacc_colors is a named vector, “Yes” is always blue, “No” orange, and “Unknown” gray.











Note📖 Good to know




About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of color-vision deficiency, so in a room of 30 people, someone probably can’t tell red from green.
Don’t rely on color alone: clear titles, axis labels, and a sensible order make a plot readable even in black and white.
crumbs: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
Epicurve by outcome

👀 Follow along 5.3 — Fill the epicurve by outcome with outcome_colors.


linelist %>%
  filter(onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = onset_date, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = outcome_colors) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  labs(x = "Week of onset", y = "Number of cases", fill = "Outcome") +
  theme_minimal()














Note🔍 What this code does




fill = outcome inside aes() splits each week’s bar by outcome, and scale_fill_manual(values = outcome_colors) uses the same colors as in Part 4.
The fixed fill = "#2a78d6" is gone from geom_histogram(). A fixed fill there would paint every bar blue and hide the outcome colors.









Important✏️ TRY IT 5 (5 min): the measles epicurve



Make a weekly epicurve of measles report_date, filled by vaccinated, with vacc_colors and scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b"). Save it as measles_epicurve — you will need it in Part 7. Hint: filter(!is.na(report_date)) first. When did the outbreak peak?
✅ Check: the peak is in the second half of March (about 115 cases in one week)






NoteShow solution






measles_epicurve <- measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(report_date)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = report_date, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vacc_colors) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "Measles cases by week of report, 2024",
    x     = "Week of report",
    y     = "Number of cases",
    fill  = "Vaccinated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

measles_epicurve








The outbreak peaked in the second half of March 2024, with 117 cases in the peak week. Saving the plot as an object means it only appears when you print it (the last line).











Note📖 Good to know




Which date? Epicurves usually use the date of symptom onset, because it’s closest to when people were infected. The date a case was reported comes later, and the delay varies from case to case.
The last weeks often look lower than they really are. Recent cases may not have been reported yet. Keep that in mind before saying an outbreak is ending.

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
⬇ Student script ⬇ Solutions ⬇ Workshop folder (ZIP)
Where this session fits. Today covers Summarize and Save and share (highlighted): turning thousands of rows into counts, percentages, and statistics, and saving a finished table to Word.
There are many packages for summary tables. This session uses three that cover almost every need: dplyr (count()/summarise()) for flexible summaries you can plot, janitor (tabyl()) for quick cross-tabs, and gtsummary for tables you publish.

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
Counts and cross-tabs

👀 Follow along 3.1 — count(outcome), then count(age_cat, outcome).


linelist %>% count(outcome)

  outcome    n
1 Recover 2158

# Two columns: every combination
linelist %>% count(age_cat, outcome)

Note🔍 What this code does




count(outcome) gives one row per outcome: Recover 2158, Death 2840, Unknown 1453. The rows follow the factor order you set in Part 2.
count(age_cat, outcome) counts every combination of age group and outcome that occurs: 24 rows. Combinations with no cases, such as 80+ and Death, are left out.

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
Percentages
count() makes a column called n. Divide by the total to get a proportion, and use scales::percent() to show it nicely:

👀 Follow along 3.2 — Add a percent column to count(outcome).


linelist %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(percent = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1))

  outcome    n percent
1 Recover 2158   33.5%
2   Death 2840   44.0%
3 Unknown 1453   22.5%








Note🔍 What this code does




count(outcome) puts the counts in a column called n.
Inside mutate(), sum(n) is the total of that column (6451), so n / sum(n) is each outcome’s share: 2840 / 6451 = 0.440 for Death.
scales::percent(..., accuracy = 0.1) shows 0.440 as “44.0%”. accuracy = 0.1 means one decimal place. The result is text: easy to read, but not for further calculations.

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
Percentages within groups: group_by()
group_by() makes the next steps happen separately for each group. Here, sum(n) becomes the total within each age group, so each age group adds up to 100%:

👀 Follow along 3.3 — Percentages within each age group with group_by().


linelist %>%
  group_by(age_cat) %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(percent = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) %>%
  ungroup()

# A tibble: 24 × 4
   age_cat  outcome     n percent
   <fct>    <fct>   <int> <chr>  
 1 Under 18 Recover  1322 33.4%  
 2 Under 18 Death    1755 44.3%  
 3 Under 18 Unknown   885 22.3%  
 4 18-29    Recover   498 34.2%  
 5 18-29    Death     648 44.5%  
 6 18-29    Unknown   309 21.2%  
 7 30-39    Recover   179 30.8%  
 8 30-39    Death     256 44.0%  
 9 30-39    Unknown   147 25.3%  
10 40-49    Recover    85 34.7%  
# ℹ 14 more rows








Note🔍 What this code does




group_by(age_cat) splits the rows into one group per age group. The data looks the same, but the next steps run once for each group.
count(outcome) then counts the outcomes inside each age group.
In mutate(), sum(n) is now the total of that age group, so each age group adds up to 100%. For example, 44.3% of the under-18s died (1755 of 3962).
ungroup() removes the grouping, so later steps work on all the rows again.









Note🤔 Think about it: how is this different from count(age_cat, outcome) without group_by()?





Without grouping, the percentages are out of all 6,451 cases, so all the rows together add up to 100%. With group_by(age_cat), each age group adds up to 100% on its own.









Tipungroup() when you’re done



A grouped data frame stays grouped. End with ungroup() so later steps don’t surprise you.








Note🔁 The base R way: table() and prop.table()



Base R makes a cross-table with table() (from Session 1), and turns it into proportions with prop.table(). margin = 1 makes each row add up to 1, like group_by(age_cat) above:

🔁 Follow along 3.4 — The base R way: table() of age group by outcome, then prop.table(margin = 1).


age_outcome <- table(linelist$age_cat, linelist$outcome)
age_outcome

          
           Recover Death Unknown
  Under 18    1322  1755     885
  18-29        498   648     309
  30-39        179   256     147
  40-49         85   105      55
  50-59         24    29      24
  60-69         16     8       3
  70-79          3     3       0
  80+            1     0       0
  Unknown       30    36      30

round(prop.table(age_outcome, margin = 1) * 100, 1)

          
           Recover Death Unknown
  Under 18    33.4  44.3    22.3
  18-29       34.2  44.5    21.2
  30-39       30.8  44.0    25.3
  40-49       34.7  42.9    22.4
  50-59       31.2  37.7    31.2
  60-69       59.3  29.6    11.1
  70-79       50.0  50.0     0.0
  80+        100.0   0.0     0.0
  Unknown     31.2  37.5    31.2








Note🔍 What this code does




table(linelist$age_cat, linelist$outcome) makes a cross-table: age groups down the side, outcomes across the top, and a count in each cell. It’s saved as age_outcome so you can reuse it.
prop.table(age_outcome, margin = 1) divides each cell by its row total, so each row adds up to 1. * 100 and round(..., 1) turn that into percentages: the same numbers as the group_by() version (44.3 for Under 18 and Death).
Unlike count(), table() shows combinations with no cases as 0.



The result is a table, not a data frame, so it doesn’t work with filter(), mutate(), or ggplot. That is why we use count() in this workshop.








Important✏️ TRY IT 3 (5 min): vaccination coverage




What percentage of measles cases were vaccinated?
Within each age group, what percentage were vaccinated? Which age group has the lowest percentage?

✅ Check: a) Yes 23.8% b) 10-14 is lowest at 21.2%

  count(vaccinated) %>%

# b)

  group_by(age_cat) %>%
  count(vaccinated) %>%
  mutate(percent = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) %>%
  ungroup()

# A tibble: 15 × 4
   age_cat vaccinated     n percent

 1 Under 5 Yes           83 22.5%

Fewer than a quarter of all cases were vaccinated. In b), each age group adds up to 100%, so you can compare groups: 10-14 year olds have the lowest coverage, at 21.2%.











Note📖 Good to know




Always ask “percent of what?” Of all cases, of each age group, or only of cases with a known value? Here the “Unknown” outcomes are part of the total, so leaving them out would change every percentage.
scales::percent() gives text. To plot or calculate with a percentage, keep the plain proportion (n / sum(n)) as well.

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
By group
Add group_by() first to get one row per group:

👀 Follow along 4.2 — The same by outcome, plus the mean BMI and mean temperature.


linelist %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    mean_age   = mean(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_age = median(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi   = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_temp  = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  outcome     n mean_age median_age mean_bmi mean_temp
  <fct>   <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Recover  2158     16.1         13     30.6      38.6
2 Death    2840     15.9         13     30.7      38.6
3 Unknown  1453     16.2         14     30.4      38.6








Tip🧩 Reading a function call



Here is a shorter version of the code above, taken apart:
linelist %>% group_by(outcome) %>% summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age_years, na.rm = TRUE))








Piece
What it is
What it does




linelist
the data
where the steps start


%>%
the pipe
passes the result on its left into the next function, as its first argument


group_by(outcome)
a dplyr function
splits the rows into one group per outcome


summarise(...)
a dplyr function
collapses each group into one row of results


n = n()
a new column called n, made by the function n()
counts the rows in each group


mean_age = mean(age_years, ...)
a new column called mean_age, made by mean()
the average age in each group


na.rm = TRUE
a named argument of mean()
“remove NAs”: skip the missing ages



Inside summarise(), the name on the left of = is the new column, and the calculation is on the right. With the pipe, R runs the steps from left to right. Read each %>% as “and then”: “take linelist, and then group it by outcome, and then summarise: n is the number of rows, and mean_age is the mean of age_years, skipping missing values.”








Note🔍 What this code does




group_by(outcome) before summarise() gives one row per outcome instead of one row for everyone.
Each row is calculated only from its own group: 2158 patients who recovered, 2840 who died, and 1453 with an unknown outcome.
In this fictional dataset the groups are very similar: the median age is 13 for both recovered and died, and the mean temperature is 38.6 °C in all three groups.









NoteUseful summary functions



Centre: mean(), median() · Spread: sd(), IQR(), min(), max(), quantile(x, 0.25) · Counts: n(), n_distinct(), sum(is.na(x))

The same calculation on many columns: across()
You met across() in Session 3. In summarise() it saves a lot of typing:

👀 Follow along 4.3 — across(): the mean of age_years, bmi, and temp by outcome.


linelist %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(across(c(age_years, bmi, temp), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  outcome age_years   bmi  temp
  <fct>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Recover      16.1  30.6  38.6
2 Death        15.9  30.7  38.6
3 Unknown      16.2  30.4  38.6








Note🔍 What this code does




across(c(age_years, bmi, temp), ...) does the same calculation on each of the three columns.
~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE) is the calculation. The ~ starts a short formula, and .x stands for “the current column”: first age_years, then bmi, then temp.
The results keep the original column names, so each of age_years, bmi, and temp now holds a mean.

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
Percentages of “yes”
fever == "yes" is TRUE or FALSE for each row (vectorization, from Session 4). sum() counts the TRUEs, and mean() gives the proportion that are TRUE:

👀 Follow along 4.4 — The percentage with fever, cough, and vomiting by outcome, with round(mean(fever == "yes") * 100, 1).


linelist %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    n_cases   = n(),
    n_fever   = sum(fever == "yes"),
    pct_fever = round(mean(fever == "yes") * 100, 1),
    pct_cough = round(mean(cough == "yes") * 100, 1),
    pct_vomit = round(mean(vomit == "yes") * 100, 1)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  outcome n_cases n_fever pct_fever pct_cough pct_vomit
  <fct>     <int>   <int>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Recover    2158    1708      79.1      82        47.9
2 Death      2840    2245      79        82.9      48.8
3 Unknown    1453    1124      77.4      84.2      46.5








Note🔍 What this code does




fever == "yes" is TRUE for each patient with fever and FALSE for everyone else.
sum(fever == "yes") counts the TRUEs (each TRUE counts as 1): 1708 of the patients who recovered had fever.
mean(fever == "yes") is the share that are TRUE: 1708 / 2158 = 0.791. * 100 and round(..., 1) turn that into 79.1.
Patients whose fever is “Unknown” count as “not yes”, so these percentages are out of all patients in the group.









Note🔁 The base R way: tapply() and aggregate()



Two base R functions do what group_by() + summarise() does for one statistic:

🔁 Follow along 4.5 — The base R way: median age by outcome with tapply() and aggregate().


tapply(linelist$age_years, linelist$outcome, median, na.rm = TRUE)   # a named vector

Recover   Death Unknown 
     13      13      14 

aggregate(age_years ~ outcome, data = linelist, FUN = median)        # a data frame

  outcome age_years
1 Recover        13
2   Death        13
3 Unknown        14








Note🔍 What this code does




tapply(linelist$age_years, linelist$outcome, median, na.rm = TRUE) splits age_years by outcome and runs median() on each piece. The result is a named vector: 13, 13, 14.
aggregate(age_years ~ outcome, data = linelist, FUN = median) gives the same medians as a data frame. Read age_years ~ outcome as “age_years by outcome”.
Before calculating, aggregate() quietly leaves out the 96 rows with no age. Here that doesn’t change the medians.



Read tapply(X, GROUP, FUNCTION) as “apply FUNCTION to X, split by GROUP”. aggregate() with a formula silently drops rows with a missing value, one reason summarise() (where you choose with na.rm) is clearer.








TipSave summaries as objects



Every result here is a data frame. Save it with <- and you can plot it (Sessions 6 and 7), join it, or export it like any other data.








Important✏️ TRY IT 4 (4 min): statistics by outcome



For each measles outcome, calculate the number of cases, mean and median age, mean temperature, and mean days in hospital (careful: NAs!).
✅ Check: Recovered n = 1048, median age 7; Died n = 50, median age 5






NoteShow solution






measles %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    mean_age   = mean(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_age = median(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_temp  = mean(temp_c),
    mean_days  = mean(days_in_hospital, na.rm = TRUE)

3 Unknown      65     7.47          5      38.7      5.12


Children who died were younger than children who recovered (median age 5 vs 7). days_in_hospital is missing for patients who were never hospitalized, so it needs na.rm = TRUE.











Important✏️ TRY IT 5 (4 min): case rates by district



Calculate cases per 10,000 people by district (number of cases / population * 10000), sorted highest first.
Hint: count(district, population) gives both columns; then mutate() and arrange(desc()).
✅ Check: East has the highest rate (22.8); Central the lowest (5.2)






NoteShow solution






measles %>%
  count(district, population) %>%
  mutate(rate_per_10k = round(n / population * 10000, 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(rate_per_10k))

  district population   n rate_per_10k
1     East      98000 223         22.8
2     West      76500 170         22.2
3    South     142000 284         20.0
4    North     185000 342         18.5
5  Central     210000 110          5.2
6  Unknown         NA  34           NA


Central has the most people but the lowest rate: raw counts and rates can tell different stories. The “Unknown” district has no population, so it gets no rate.











Note📖 Good to know




Mean or median? A few large values pull the mean up, but barely move the median. Ages here are skewed toward children: the mean age is 16.1, the median 13. For skewed numbers like ages, incomes, or days in hospital, the median is usually the better summary.
n() counts all rows, including rows with missing values. To count only the non-missing values of a column, use sum(!is.na(x)).

text:
replace_na() with across()
across() applies the same function to many columns at once. Here: for every text column, replace NA with "Unknown".

👀 Follow along 5.1 — Replace NA with “Unknown” in every text column of linelist_final. Check with count(gender) and count(outcome).


linelist_final <- linelist_final %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ replace_na(.x, "Unknown")))

linelist_final %>% count(gender)

   gender    n
1 Unknown  304
2  female 3073
3    male 3074

linelist_final %>% count(outcome)

  outcome    n
1   Death 2840
2 Recover 2158
3 Unknown 1453


Read ~ replace_na(.x, "Unknown") as: “for each column (.x), replace its NAs with Unknown”. where(is.character) picks only text columns, so number and date columns keep their NAs.






Note🔍 What this code does




where(is.character) picks the text columns: case_id, outcome, gender, hospital, age_unit, hospital_name, and age_cat.
across(...) runs replace_na(.x, "Unknown") on each of them, and mutate() saves the result back into the same columns.
count(gender) now shows Unknown 304 instead of NA, and count(outcome) shows Unknown 1453. The numbers didn’t change, only the label.
Why bother? Text “Unknown” shows up in tables and plots as a category of its own, while NA is easy to drop by accident (as table() does without useNA; see Session 1).









Note



For a single column: mutate(gender = replace_na(gender, "Unknown"))

title: Session 3: Missing Data, Joins, and Export
text:
How joins work
A join combines two data frames by matching rows on a key column that both share. A tiny example first:

👀 Follow along 6.1 — A tiny example. Make patients (id 1, 2, 3) and labs (id 2, 3, 4) with tibble(), then try four joins on them.


patients <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3), name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cho"))
labs     <- tibble(id = c(2, 3, 4), result = c("positive", "negative", "positive"))

left_join(patients, labs, by = "id")    # all patients; NA where no lab result

# A tibble: 3 × 3
     id name  result  
  <dbl> <chr> <chr>   
1     1 Ana   <NA>    
2     2 Ben   positive
3     3 Cho   negative

inner_join(patients, labs, by = "id")   # only ids in BOTH

# A tibble: 2 × 3
     id name  result  
  <dbl> <chr> <chr>   
1     2 Ben   positive
2     3 Cho   negative

full_join(patients, labs, by = "id")    # everyone from both

# A tibble: 4 × 3
     id name  result  
  <dbl> <chr> <chr>   
1     1 Ana   <NA>    
2     2 Ben   positive
3     3 Cho   negative
4     4 <NA>  positive

anti_join(patients, labs, by = "id")    # patients with NO lab result

# A tibble: 1 × 2
     id name 
  <dbl> <chr>
1     1 Ana  








Note🔍 What this code does




tibble() makes a small data frame by hand, like data.frame() in the Session 1 diagram.
patients has ids 1, 2, 3 and labs has ids 2, 3, 4, so ids 2 and 3 are in both, 1 is only in patients, and 4 is only in labs.
left_join() keeps all 3 patients; Ana (id 1) gets NA for result because she has no lab. inner_join() keeps only the 2 ids in both. full_join() keeps all 4 ids. anti_join() returns the 1 patient with no lab.
by = "id" names the key: the column used to match rows. It must exist in both data frames.











Join
Keeps
A question it answers




left_join()
every row of the first data frame
Add each patient’s lab result, if there is one


right_join()
every row of the second data frame
(the same as left_join() with the two swapped)


inner_join()
only rows that match in both
Patients who have a lab result, with the result


full_join()
every row from both
Everyone in either list


semi_join()
rows of the first with a match, adding no columns
Which patients have a lab result?


anti_join()
rows of the first with no match
Which patients are missing a lab result? Great for checking



left_join() is the one you will use most: start with your main dataset and add information to it.






Note🔁 The base R way: merge() and %in%



Base R joins with one function, merge(). The all arguments choose the type of join (reading only, you don’t need to type this):

merge(patients, labs, by = "id")                # inner join (the default!)

  id name   result
1  2  Ben positive
2  3  Cho negative

merge(patients, labs, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)  # left join

  id name   result
1  1  Ana     <NA>
2  2  Ben positive
3  3  Cho negative

merge(patients, labs, by = "id", all = TRUE)    # full join

  id name   result
1  1  Ana     <NA>
2  2  Ben positive
3  3  Cho negative
4  4 <NA> positive


Watch out: merge() keeps only matching rows unless you say otherwise, and it sorts the result by the key. %in% asks “is each value found in the other vector?”, and gives one TRUE/FALSE per value. It is the base R way to find rows with no match:

patients$id %in% labs$id

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE

patients[!patients$id %in% labs$id, ]   # the same as anti_join()

# A tibble: 1 × 2
     id name 
  <dbl> <chr>
1     1 Ana  








Note🔍 What this code does




merge(patients, labs, by = "id") gives 2 rows: like inner_join(), it keeps only the matches unless you ask for more. all.x = TRUE keeps every row of the first data frame (a left join), and all = TRUE keeps every row of both (a full join).
patients$id %in% labs$id checks each patient id against the lab ids: FALSE TRUE TRUE (only id 1 has no lab).
! flips that to TRUE FALSE FALSE, and patients[ROWS, ] keeps the rows where it’s TRUE: Ana. The empty space after the comma means “all columns”. You’ll learn this bracket style in Session 4.



%in% is worth learning well: you will use it inside filter() too, for example filter(district %in% c("North", "South")).

Tip🧩 Reading a function call

Piece
What it is

linelist_final %>%

title: Session 3: Missing Data, Joins, and Export
text:
Check the join
Always check the number of rows. A left join should not add rows — if it does, the key appears more than once in the second data frame.

👀 Follow along 6.3 — Check the join with nrow() and anti_join().


nrow(linelist_final)

[1] 6451

nrow(combined_linelist)

[1] 6451

# Cases with no matching case_info (should be 0)
anti_join(linelist_final, case_info, by = "case_id") %>% nrow()

[1] 0

sum(!linelist_final$case_id %in% case_info$case_id)   # the same check in base R

[1] 0

# Is case_id unique in case_info?
case_info %>% get_dupes(case_id) %>% nrow()

[1] 0


Same number of rows before and after, every case matched, and case_id is unique in case_info: the join worked.






Note🔍 What this code does




The two nrow() lines both give 6451: the join added columns, not rows.
anti_join(linelist_final, case_info, by = "case_id") returns the cases that found no match in case_info; nrow() counts them: 0. The %in% line does the same check in base R and also gives 0.
get_dupes(case_id) on case_info finds no repeated IDs (it prints “No duplicate combinations found” and returns 0 rows). That matters: if an ID appeared twice in case_info, the left join would copy that case into two rows.









Important✏️ TRY IT 6 (4 min): join the district information



Add district_info to measles_final with left_join() (the key is district). Did the number of rows change? Which rows got no population, and why?
Pattern: anti_join(measles_final, district_info, by = "district") %>% count(district)
✅ Check: still 1163 rows; the 34 “Unknown” district rows have no population






NoteShow solution






measles_final <- measles_final %>%
  left_join(district_info, by = "district")

nrow(measles_final)

[1] 1163

anti_join(measles_final, district_info, by = "district") %>% count(district)

  district  n
1  Unknown 34


The number of rows did not change. district_info has no “Unknown” district, so those 34 rows have no match and their population is NA.











Note📖 Good to know




Before any join, ask two questions: Is the key spelled and formatted the same way in both data frames (“ID001” won’t match “id001” or “ID 001”)? And is the key unique in the data frame you’re adding? If not, rows multiply.
When the key has different names in the two data frames, give both: by = c("case_id" = "id").
You can tell left_join() what you expect: relationship = "many-to-one" means “each row of the first data frame matches at most one row of the second”. In combined_linelist, some case IDs appear more than once in the linelist (Part 4), but each one is in case_info only once. If case_info ever had a repeated ID, R would stop with an error (“Each row in x must match at most 1 row in y”) instead of quietly adding rows.
Joins are how you link different sources: lab results to patients, census figures to counties, survey answers to participants.

text:
Objects and the assignment arrow <-
<- stores a value in an object so you can use it later. Read it as “gets”. The object appears in the Variables pane. Shortcut: Option + - (Mac) or Alt + - (Windows) types <- for you.

👀 Follow along 1.1 — Store a number in an object called my_age, then add 5 to it.
Pattern: OBJECT_NAME <- VALUE


my_age <- 35
my_age

[1] 35

my_age + 5

[1] 40








Note🔍 What this code does




my_age <- 35 creates an object called my_age and stores the number 35 in it. Nothing prints: saving is silent. my_age now appears in the Variables pane.
my_age on its own prints what is stored: [1] 35. The [1] means “this is the first value”. It helps you keep your place when the output runs over several lines.
my_age + 5 uses the object in a calculation and prints 40. my_age itself is still 35: to change it, you would save again with <-.

title: Session 1: R Basics, Importing, and Inspecting Data
text:
Vectors
c() combines values into a vector. Every value in a vector has the same type. Text values need quotes: c("Central Hospital", "Other").

👀 Follow along 1.2 — Make a vector of ages with c(), then find the mean().


ages <- c(2, 18, 56, 61)
mean(ages)

[1] 34.25








Note🔍 What this code does




c(2, 18, 56, 61) combines four numbers into one vector, and ages <- saves it.
mean(ages) gives the whole vector to mean(), which adds the values and divides by how many there are: (2 + 18 + 56 + 61) / 4 = 34.25.
Most R functions work on a whole vector at once, so you rarely handle values one by one.

title: Session 1: R Basics, Importing, and Inspecting Data
text:
Functions and arguments
A function does something to its inputs (arguments): function_name(argument1, argument2, ...). Arguments can be named.

👀 Follow along 1.3 — Use round(3.14159) with and without digits = 2.


round(3.14159)

[1] 3

round(3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14








Note🔍 What this code does




round(3.14159) has one argument, the number. The digits argument wasn’t given, so round() uses its default, 0, and rounds to a whole number: 3.
round(3.14159, digits = 2) adds a second, named argument and gives 3.14.
Arguments you leave out use their default value. The help page (?round) lists every argument and its default.









TipGetting help



Type ?round in the Console to open the help page for any function.

title: Session 1: R Basics, Importing, and Inspecting Data
text:
Data frames
A data frame is a table: each column is a variable (a vector), each row is an observation. (Later you’ll also see tibbles: the tidyverse version of a data frame, which prints more neatly.)
Here is a small data frame called patients, drawn as boxes. Each column is a vector, so every value in it has the same type: name is all text and age is all numbers. Each row is one patient.

  
    name
    "Ana""Ben""Cho"
    text
  
  
    age
    345127
    numbers
  

This is the code that makes it. You don’t need to type it: you’ll build data frames yourself in Session 4. Notice $, which pulls out one column; you’ll use it often.

patients <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cho"),
  age  = c(34, 51, 27)
)
patients

  name age
1  Ana  34
2  Ben  51
3  Cho  27

patients$age        # $ pulls out one column

[1] 34 51 27








WarningCommon mistakes




R is case-sensitive: Age and age are different
Object names can’t start with a number or contain spaces: age2 and my_age work, 2age and my age don’t. Avoid names R already uses, such as c, mean, or data
Text needs quotes ("Central Hospital"); object names do not (my_age)
Every ( needs a ) — Positron highlights the matching pair
# starts a comment; R ignores the rest of the line









Important✏️ TRY IT 1 (2 min): objects and functions



Store three temperatures, 38.5, 39.1, and 37.9, in an object called my_temps. Then find their mean().
✅ Check: the mean is 38.5






NoteShow solution






my_temps <- c(38.5, 39.1, 37.9)
mean(my_temps)

[1] 38.5













Note📖 Good to know




Script or Console? The Console runs a line once and forgets it. Your script is the record of what you did, so type your code in the script and run it from there.
Objects live in R’s memory, not on your disk. They disappear when you close Positron or restart R. That’s fine: rerun your script and they’re back. If you’re ever asked whether to save the workspace, choose No.
<- or =? Both can store a value, but this course always uses <-, so that = only ever means “name an argument” (as in digits = 2).
A vector holds one type. If you mix text into numbers, R turns everything into text: c(5, 12, "unknown") is three pieces of text. You’ll see this in the practice data, where a few ages say “unknown”.

title: Session 1: R Basics, Importing, and Inspecting Data
text:
Error, warning, or message?
You just saw red text in the Console. Red text comes in three kinds, and each one asks something different of you:









Kind
How to spot it
What happened
What to do




Error
starts with Error
R stopped. The line did nothing.
Read the message, fix the code, run it again


Warning
starts with Warning
R finished, but something may be off
Check the result: did values turn into NA, or did rows disappear?


Message
anything else, like the list from library(tidyverse)
Information only
Nothing



The message after Error usually tells you what’s wrong, for example could not find function "Count" (R is case-sensitive: the function is count()). You’ll practise reading them in TRY IT 5.






TipAsking for help



Stuck? Put up your red sticky note. When you ask someone for help, in class, by email, or online, include three things:

Which line you ran (copy it)
What you expected to happen
The exact message R gave you (copy it, don’t retype it)









Note📖 Good to know




Packages are shared on CRAN, R’s official package library, which has more than 20,000 of them. install.packages() downloads from there.
The tidyverse is a family of packages designed to work together, with the same style of function names and arguments. That’s why one library(tidyverse) loads several of them.

title: Session 1: R Basics, Importing, and Inspecting Data
text:
Relative vs absolute paths

Bad (absolute): "/Users/mwegener/Desktop/maybe_here/data.csv" — only works on one computer
Good (relative): here("raw_data", "data.csv") — works on any computer that has the project folder

here() finds the top of the project folder (it looks for a .here file, which the workshop folder has) and builds the path from there.

👀 Follow along 3.1 — Find the top of the project folder.
Pattern: here::here()


here::here()                                   # where is the top of my project?







Note🔍 What this code does




here::here() prints the full path to the top of the project folder: wherever you saved cwml-r-workshop on your computer. It finds the top by looking for the .here file.
If the path isn’t your workshop folder, the folder isn’t open in Positron. Choose File → Open Folder… and open it.




👀 Follow along 3.2 — Build the path to raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx.
Pattern: here::here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.EXTENSION")


here::here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx")    # full path to a file inside it







Note🔍 What this code does




here::here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx") adds a folder and a file name to that path, joined with /. R uses / on every computer, Windows included.
It only builds the path, as text. It doesn’t check that the file exists or open it: that’s the job of import(), next.
Each piece is in quotes because it’s text, not the name of an object.



here::here() means “the here() function from the here package”. The :: lets you use a function before loading its package.






Note📖 Good to know




The working directory is the folder R reads files from and saves files to. Opening the workshop folder in Positron sets it for you.
Older tutorials often start with setwd("C:/Users/..."). That path only exists on one computer, so the script breaks everywhere else. A project folder with here() avoids this.
here() finds the top of the project by looking for a marker: a .here file (the workshop folder has one), an .Rproj file, or a .git folder.

title: Session 1: R Basics, Importing, and Inspecting Data
text:
import() + here()
rio::import() reads almost any file type (.csv, .xlsx, .txt, SPSS, Stata, SAS, …). It works out the type from the file extension, so you only need to learn one function. Save the result with <-, or it only prints to the Console and is gone.

👀 Follow along 4.1 — Import raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx and call it linelist_raw.
Pattern: NEW_NAME <- import(here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.EXTENSION"))


linelist_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx"))







Tip🧩 Reading a function call



Here is the line you just ran, taken apart:
linelist_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx"))








Piece
What it is
What it does




linelist_raw
the name of a new object
holds the result


<-
the assignment arrow
saves the result in linelist_raw


import(...)
a function from the rio package
reads a file into R


here(...)
a function from the here package, used as the argument of import()
builds the full path to the file


"raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx"
two text arguments of here()
the folder, then the file name



R runs it from the inside out: first here() builds the path, then import() reads the file at that path, and finally <- saves the result. Reading code aloud in the same order helps: “linelist_raw gets: import the file at here, raw_data, linelist_raw.xlsx.”








Note🔍 What this code does




import() saw the .xlsx ending and read the file as an Excel workbook (the first sheet, unless you ask for another).
Nothing prints. linelist_raw appears in the Variables pane with 6604 rows and 12 columns.
The result is a data frame: the same kind of table as patients in Part 1, only bigger. Each row is one patient (a case), and each column is one piece of information about them.









WarningCommon mistakes




File names must match exactly, including capitals and the extension.
“Error: No such file” means the folder or file name is misspelled, or the workshop folder isn’t open (check the Explorer on the left).









TipOther import options you may see




Base R: read.csv() — older, slower, and needs more settings
readr: read_csv() — the tidyverse version, fast and returns a tibble
haven: read_sav(), read_dta(), read_sas() — SPSS, Stata, SAS files
Excel files with several sheets: import(here("raw_data", "file.xlsx"), which = "Sheet2")









Important✏️ TRY IT 2 (2 min): import the practice data



Import the practice data raw_data/measles_raw.csv and call it measles_raw.
✅ Check: in the Variables pane, measles_raw shows 1215 rows and 11 columns






NoteShow solution






measles_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "measles_raw.csv"))












Note📖 Good to know




import() passes the work to a specialist package based on the file ending: readxl for Excel, data.table for CSV and text files, and haven for SPSS, Stata, and SAS. You only need to remember one function.
import() returns a plain data frame, which prints every row. That’s why this lesson wraps long output in head(). Tidyverse functions return a tibble, a data frame that prints only the first 10 rows.
Excel stores dates as date-times, so most date columns arrive as <dttm>. One column, date.onset, arrives as text: Excel files often hold surprises like this, which is why you inspect before you clean.

Note🔍 What this code does

The hospital list shows the same hospital spelled several ways, for example “Central Hospital” (457 rows) and “Central Hopital” (11). R treats every spelling as a different hospital, so these have to be fixed before counting cases per hospital. 1509 rows have no hospital at all.
count(linelist_raw, age_unit) shows that 37 ages are in months, not years.









Note🔁 The base R way: table()



You will often see base R’s table() in other people’s code. It counts too, but it hides missing values unless you ask for them. (Reading only: you don’t need to type this.)

table(linelist_raw$OUTCOME)                   # where are the missing outcomes?

Note🔍 What this code does




table() takes one column, pulled out with $, instead of the data and a column name.
Without useNA = "ifany", it shows only Death (2898) and Recover (2213). The 1493 missing outcomes are left out without a warning, so any percentages you worked out from it would be wrong.
useNA = "ifany" adds an <NA> count whenever there are missing values.

text:
Teaching notes by part
Part 1 — Set up. Same import pipeline as Session 6. Point out why we save vacc_colors now: every plot later in the session reuses it, so “Yes” is always the same blue.
Part 2 — geom_bar(). Start with x = hospital_name so learners see the overlapping labels, then switch to y. Ask the class: which version (stack, fill, or dodge) answers “do older patients die more often?” — the 100% "fill" version; the stacked one mostly shows that there are many more young patients.
Part 3 — geom_col(). Ask the class: the 70–79 and 80+ bars are based on very few patients — check n in death_by_age. How much should we trust them? — Not much: 70–79 has 6 patients and 80+ has 1 (0% died).
Part 4 — Choosing colors. The original workshop used red/green and dark red/red. These pages use blue, orange, and gray (#2a78d6, #eb6834, #9a9a95); blue, orange, and aqua (#2a78d6, #eb6834, #1baf7a) stay distinguishable for the common types of color blindness. For more colors, the viridis scales are built in: scale_fill_viridis_d().
Part 5 — Epidemic curves. Show the full-range epicurve first and ask the class: what is going on before 2014? — 538 onset dates fall in 2012–2013 (April 2012 – April 2013), long before the outbreak, and every one belongs to a case ID that appears more than once (the duplicate IDs from Session 3), usually with the same day and month but a different year. Almost certainly data-entry errors. Make the point: plots reveal problems tables hide.
Part 6 — Facets. Point out that facets share axes by default, which is what makes them comparable; scales = "free_y" breaks that. In TRY IT 6, district peaks are close but not identical with weekly bins (Central and North peak the week of 17 March, East the week of 24 March, West 10 March, and South is nearly flat from early March into April) — “they all peak in March” is the fair answer.
Part 7 — Saving plots. Have learners open the saved PNG from the Explorer (outputs/ folder) — text size in the file often looks different from the Plots pane; adjust width/height to fix it.
Wrap-up. Recap the journey: problem list (S1) → cleaning pipeline (S2) → de-duplicated, joined file (S3) → vectors, subsetting, reshaping (S4) → summary tables and Table 1 (S5) → histograms, scatter, box plots (S6) → bar charts, epicurves, facets saved to files (S7). Session 8 (Programming) is optional: functions, if/else, and loops — for example, one epicurve per hospital automatically. Encourage learners to repeat the whole workflow on their own data.

title: Instructor notes: Session 5
text:
Teaching notes by part
Overview — why these three packages. There are many packages for summary tables (base R summary() and table(), psych::describe(), rstatix::get_summary_stats(), …). This session teaches three that cover almost every need: dplyr (count()/summarise()) for flexible summaries you can plot, janitor (tabyl()) for quick cross-tabs, and gtsummary for tables you publish. Say this up front if learners ask “why not X?”.
Part 1 — Set up. Remind learners this is the dataset finished in Session 3: cleaned, de-duplicated, and joined to the case information (symptoms and temperature). They can confirm the import in the Variables pane.
Part 2 — Factors. Run count(age_cat) before relevelling and ask learners what’s wrong with the order (“Under 18” sorts after “80+”). Emphasize that the order carries through to plots too — they’ll see it again in Sessions 6 and 7. Note: the .rds files saved in Session 3 contain plain text columns, not factors, so the order has to be set again after every import (the student script says this; the original instructor script implied the .rds already kept the order). A misspelled level gives an “Unknown levels” warning and is silently ignored.
Part 3 — Counting and percentages. After the group_by(age_cat) %>% count(outcome) example, ask the class:

How is this different from count(age_cat, outcome) without group_by()? — Without grouping, the percentages are out of all 6,451 cases, so all rows together add up to 100%. With grouping, each age group adds up to 100%.

Stress ungroup(): a grouped data frame stays grouped and can surprise them later.
Part 4 — summarise(). Show what happens without na.rm = TRUE (the whole result becomes NA). Connect mean(fever == "yes") to Session 4’s vectorization: TRUE/FALSE, sum() counts the TRUEs, mean() gives the proportion. In TRY IT 4 (statistics by outcome), days_in_hospital needs na.rm = TRUE because non-hospitalized patients have NA. In TRY IT 5 (district rates), point out that Central has the most people but the lowest rate — counts and rates tell different stories — and that the “Unknown” district gets no rate.
Part 5 — tabyl(). Spend a moment on the order of the adorn_ functions — totals must come before percentages because they need the raw counts. TRY IT 6 (vaccination and death: 6.3% vs 0.7%) is a good moment to discuss what this data does and doesn’t show: it’s fictional practice data, the numbers of deaths are small (2 vaccinated deaths), and a crude cross-tab doesn’t adjust for anything (e.g. age).
Part 6 — Table 1. Explain why we turn “Unknown” back into NA with na_if(): in Session 3 we replaced NA with “Unknown” so missing values show up in counts, but tbl_summary() has its own Missing row. na_if() with where(is.character) only touches text columns, so factor columns (age_cat, vaccinated) keep “Unknown” as a category. Mention add_p() but only for analyses where a statistical test is planned. The Word export uses as_flex_table() %>% flextable::save_as_docx(); have learners find outputs/table1.docx in the Explorer and open it. For the measles Table 1, point out that “Missing” days in hospital means not hospitalized, not lost data.
Wrap-up. Recap: fct_relevel(), count(), group_by(), summarise(), across(), tabyl() + adorn_*(), tbl_summary(). Preview Session 6 — Plotting basics: ggplot2 from the ground up — histograms, scatter plots, and box plots.
🔁 Base R boxes (about 2 minutes each). Three short demos: factor(), table() + prop.table(), and tapply() / aggregate(). The goal is reading knowledge: learners will meet these in papers’ code, help pages, and AI answers. One point per box: factor() turns misspelled levels into NA without a warning; a table is not a data frame; aggregate() drops rows with missing values. If time is short, show them as “here’s what this looks like in base R” without asking learners to type along.

text:
Teaching notes by part
Part 1 — Set up. The library() and import() lines are already in the student script: learners just run them. Only the measles imports (TRY IT 1) are typed. Explain trust = TRUE briefly (an .rds can contain R code; we made these files ourselves). If a learner’s measles_clean.rds is missing or broken, they can download a fresh copy from GitHub.
Part 2 — Where is data missing? Ask the class: is every missing value a mistake? — No. date_of_outcome is missing for patients with no outcome yet (real information); bmi is missing where Session 2 set impossible values to NA; a missing case_id is a problem because those rows can’t be linked. The drop_na(bmi) example is reading only: point to it on screen 2. It would lose 1382 of 6604 patients.
Part 3 — Rows with no ID. The new IDs are simply paste0("ID", row_number()): ID1 to ID130. If learners look lost, run paste0("ID", 1) in the Console first. Zero-padding with sprintf() (so ID2 sorts before ID10) is in the 📖 box at the end of Part 3: mention it in one sentence.
Part 4 — Duplicates. After distinct(), get_dupes(case_id) still finds 1106 rows whose ID appears more than once. These rows are not exact copies, so distinct() keeps them. In a real project you would ask the data owner which record is correct. We keep them for this workshop, but it’s a good discussion point: cleaning often needs people, not just code.
Part 5 — Replacing missing values. Point out that where(is.character) skips number and date columns, so they keep their NAs — which is what we want.
Part 6 — Joining datasets. Draw the tiny patients/labs example on the board if you can. The old version of this workshop ran distinct() after the join. Removing duplicates before joining (Part 4) is the better habit: duplicates are easier to spot in the original data, and they can’t multiply during the join. Stress the row-count check: 6451 rows before and after. Point to the new column in the join table (“a question it answers”): semi_join() asks “which patients have a lab result?” and anti_join() “which are missing one?”. The 📖 box at the end of Part 6 shows relationship = "many-to-one", which turns a silently multiplied join into an error.

import(here("processed_data", "test.csv")) %>% filter(is.na(case_id)) %>% nrow()   # 0, not 130!
Delete test.csv afterwards.
Make sure everyone saves measles_final.rds — they need it for every remaining session. Early finishers: ⭐ Bonus (inner vs left join).

Teaching notes by part
Part 1 — R basics. Keep this brisk (about 10 minutes); learners practise all of it in every later session. Have someone make a deliberate mistake (Mean(ages)) to show that R is case-sensitive. The data frame diagram is reading only: point to it on screen 2 and explain “each column is one type”. Nobody types data.frame() today.
Part 2 — Packages, and error, warning, or message. Learners who did the setup only need the library() lines. Use the red text that library(tidyverse) just printed to introduce the table: “this red text is a message, nothing to do”. Point out the “Asking for help” box: it’s how you want questions phrased during the course.
Part 3 — Project folders and here(). Show that here::here() points at the workshop folder because it’s open in Positron (and has a .here file). There is no TRY IT here; learners use here() in the import TRY IT next.
Positron vs RStudio names: if learners follow older tutorials, Positron’s Variables pane is RStudio’s Environment pane, and the Explorer is the Files pane.
Part 5 — Inspecting. This is the longest part. Start by reading the five questions at the top of Part 5 aloud: everything after answers one of them. The “Think about it” questions on the lesson page are prompts to ask the class:

What is wrong with these column names? — spaces, dots, capitals, mixed styles.
Which column types look wrong? — date.onset is text, age is text, and age_unit hints that some ages aren’t in years.

After skim(), point at the n_missing column, the negative minimum of wt_kg, and the near-300 cm maximum of ht_cm. The 🔁 table() box and “Other ways to look” (view(), names(), head()) are reading only: mention them in one sentence each.
TRY IT 5 — fix the broken code. Give learners the time to struggle a little, then go through the four lines together and read each message aloud. The point of line 4 is that a warning can reveal a data problem rather than a typo.
Part 6 — The problem list. Build the list with the class: ask learners to call out what they found before showing the table. The “Fixed in” column previews Session 2. Duplicates are on the list as “not checked yet”: Session 3 checks them.

title: R Hands-on Workshop Series
text:
Welcome! This hands-on workshop teaches you to analyze data in R using the tidyverse, and the base R foundations underneath it: vectors, types, subsetting, lists, and functions. Each lesson also shows the base R version of key tidyverse steps, so you can read other people’s code (see Base R ↔︎ tidyverse). You will take a realistic, messy outbreak dataset all the way from the raw file to clean data, summary tables, and publication-ready plots — and finish by writing your own functions and loops.
No experience with R or programming is needed.

title: R Hands-on Workshop Series
text:
What you’ll learn

Set up a project folder and import data from almost any file type
Inspect a dataset and find its problems before you analyze it
Clean messy data: fix column names, types, misspellings, impossible values, and duplicates
Handle missing values and join datasets together
Understand how R stores data (vectors, lists, data frames), and reshape it between wide and long
Read base R code and translate it to the tidyverse (and back)
Summarize data and make a publication-ready “Table 1”
Make histograms, scatter plots, box plots, bar charts, and epidemic curves with ggplot2
Write your own functions and loops to automate repeated work

text: This guide is for anyone teaching the workshop. The lessons contain everything learners see; the pages here add timing, teaching notes, and answers to the questions to ask the class.

title: Instructor Guide
text:
The teaching rhythm
Every part of every lesson follows the same three steps:

👀 Follow along — you live-code the new skill on the workshop dataset (the outbreak linelist). Learners type the same code into their student script.
✏️ TRY IT — learners immediately do the same thing on the practice dataset (the measles outbreak). Each TRY IT takes 1–10 minutes and has a ✅ Check so learners know they got it right.
Show the answer (or ask a learner to show theirs), then move on.

This is the approach used by The Carpentries: short demonstrations followed straight away by practice, so problems surface while they are still easy to fix.

title: Instructor Guide
text:
Teaching with two instructors
The workshop is taught by two instructors with two screens: screen 1 shows Positron, screen 2 shows the lesson page on this website. Give each instructor a clear role, so learners never have to choose whom to listen to.









Lead
Co-instructor

Questions

Don’t explain to the whole room while the other instructor is typing. Save asides for a TRY IT, when everyone is working on their own anyway.
Point to the numbers: “we’re on Follow along 3.2”, “do TRY IT 2”. Learners find the same number in their script and on screen 2.
Point to the explanations: the 🔍 “What this code does” and 📖 “Good to know” boxes explain the why, so you don’t have to say all of it out loud.


The parking lot
Keep a shared document or a whiteboard for questions that don’t belong to the current part:

Answered later today or in a later session: “Great question, we’ll get there in Session 3. I’ll park it.” Come back to it then.
Off-topic or about someone’s own data: answer it after class or by email.



Keep time
Each session’s instructor page has a Start by time for every part, and a list of what to skip when you’re behind. The co-instructor watches the clock and gives the lead a signal (“five minutes left in this part”). If you run out of time, stop at the end of a part and point learners to the rest of the lesson page. Don’t speed through the remaining parts.

Live coding tips

Type, don’t paste. Learners need to see code being written — and your typos and fixes are useful teaching moments.
Go slower than feels natural, and say what you’re typing as you type it.
Use a big font (Positron: View → Appearance → Zoom In, or Cmd/Ctrl + +) and a light color theme for the projector.
Run every line and talk about the output before moving on.
Read errors out loud and fix them together — learners will meet the same errors.

Give every learner a green and a red sticky note.

Green on the laptop = “I’m done with the TRY IT”

Start the answer when most notes are green. Helpers go to red notes first.
Aim for one helper for every 8–10 learners. Helpers don’t need to be experts — they need to have done the lesson.
Early finishers can work on the ⭐ BONUS at the end of each lesson.

title: Instructor notes: Session 2
text:
Teaching notes by part
Overall rhythm. Learners build two cleaned datasets side by side: linelist_clean with you (Follow along), and measles_clean in the TRY ITs. Both are built one step at a time: each part takes the current object, adds one fix, and saves it back with <-. Part 8 then shows the same linelist steps as one pipeline — the version you would keep in a real project. If a learner’s object gets into a bad state, they can re-run from Part 3 (linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>% clean_names()). The filled-in script is solutions/Session 2 - Cleaning_SOLUTIONS.R.
Part 1 — Set up. The library() and import() lines are already in the student script: learners just run them. Only the measles import (TRY IT 1) is typed. Briefly put up the Session 1 problem list and the “Fixed in” column; emphasize never edit the raw data file.
Part 2 — The pipe, filter(), and arrange(). All three are new today: Session 1 used one function at a time. Start from count(linelist_raw, age_unit), which learners know, and show that linelist_raw %>% count(age_unit) does the same; then read linelist_raw %>% arrange(wt_kg) %>% head(3) aloud as “and then”. Show the keyboard shortcut. filter() and arrange() find two of the problems from the Session 1 list (37 ages in months, impossible heights). select() is introduced here too. The two common slips: %>% at the start of a line, and a trailing %>% on the last line (the Console shows + and waits — press Esc).
Part 3 — Column names. Show names() before and after clean_names(). Point out that backticks are no longer needed. Stress that in rename() the new name goes on the left.
Part 4 — Types. Point out the “NAs introduced by coercion” warning when learners convert measles age_years: it is expected (the 27 “unknown” values) — a warning is not an error. The TRY IT’s summary() showing a max of 999 sets up Part 5. A common slip is forgetting the <-, so nothing is saved.
Part 5 — if_else(). Ask the class (a “Think about it” on the lesson page):

What would have happened in later analyses if we had skipped the months → years step? — A 6-month-old baby would be counted as 6 years old (37 ages are in months).

Explain why we replace impossible weights with NA rather than deleting the row: we keep the patient’s age, outcome, and dates.
🔁 ifelse() box (reading only, 30 seconds). Point to it on screen 2: “you’ll see ifelse() in other people’s code; it looks the same, but it turns dates into numbers, so use if_else().” Nobody types it. The 📖 box at the end of Part 5 mentions na_if() and coalesce() as shortcuts; mention them in one sentence.
Part 6 — case_when(). Point out that rows matching no condition become NA (gender), and that .default catches everything else (hospital). Show count(hospital, hospital_name) as the way to check every recode. Common errors: = instead of ~, a missing or extra comma. After TRY IT 6, open the 🤔 “it ran without an error, but is it right?” box: leaving "M" out of the male line silently makes 86 patients NA. This is the habit to build: check every recode. TRY IT 7 (district) is the hardest of the session and the first to become homework; a hint is to run str_to_title() first so each str_detect() only needs to catch misspellings.
Part 7 — New variables. BMI is reading only: walk through it on screen 2 in about a minute, and open the “Think about it” box (a BMI of 1,250? — the heights and weights don’t fit together, so BMIs outside 10–60 become NA). About 1,400 BMIs (1,382) end up NA because the height and weight values in this teaching dataset are unrealistic. Setting only the bad value to NA, instead of filtering out those rows, keeps everything else about the patient. BMI is in the Part 8 pipeline, so the saved file has it.
For age_cat (Follow along 7.1), point out that case_when() stops at the first TRUE line, and warn against ending with TRUE ~ "80+" / .default = "80+" — it puts missing ages into the oldest group. count() shows the groups in alphabetical order; that is fixed with factors in Session 5.
🔁 cut() box (reading only, 30 seconds). cut() is very common in epidemiology and clinical code for age groups. Point out on screen 2 that the counts match case_when(), that the groups come out in order (a factor, a preview of Session 5), and that without right = FALSE an 18-year-old goes into “Under 18”.
Part 8 — One pipeline and saving. The pipeline is already in the student script: nobody types it. Read it aloud from top to bottom, naming the part each group of lines came from, then run it. Point out that inside one mutate(), later lines can use columns made on earlier lines (bmi is created, then fixed). Make sure everyone saves measles_clean.rds — they need it in Session 3. Early finishers: the ⭐ Bonus asks them to rewrite all their measles steps as one pipeline.
Wrap-up. Today: clean_names(), rename(), mutate(), as.Date(), as.numeric(), if_else(), case_when(), str_detect(), export(). Preview Session 3 — Missing data, joins, and export: rows with no Case ID, duplicates, replacing missing values, joining case_info, and saving the final datasets.

title: Instructor notes: Session 4
text:
Teaching notes by part
Why this session matters. Sessions 1–3 used tidyverse functions that hide how R stores data. This session opens the hood. Vectors and vectorization explain why mutate() works on a whole column at once; base-R subsetting is everywhere in other people’s code, help pages, and Stack Overflow answers, and learners need it to write functions in Session 8; and reshaping is needed for many summaries and plots.
Part 2 — Vectors and types. The 📖 box at the end of Part 2 has two traps worth one sentence each: x == NA is always NA (use is.na()), and IDs with leading zeros should stay text. Point out that c(1, 2, "unknown") is exactly why one “unknown” turned the whole age column into text in Session 1. Show that ages and the other objects appear in the Variables pane, which also shows each vector’s type and length.
Part 3 — Vectorization. Stress that mutate() is just a vectorized calculation on a column — no loop needed. Point out that sum()/mean() of a comparison counts/gives proportions; they will use mean(fever == "yes") * 100 inside summarise() in Session 5.
Part 4 — Subsetting with base R. Rows first, then columns — have learners say it out loud. A common slip is forgetting the comma (df[1:3] picks columns). The mean-temperature example and the “Base R and missing values” box are reading only now: walk through the box on screen 2 slowly, because it is the point of the session. nrow(linelist[linelist$temp > 40, ]) gives 244, nrow(filter(linelist, temp > 40)) gives 93 — base R adds a row of NAs for each of the 151 missing temperatures. TRY IT 4 (c) repeats this trap on the measles data (225 vs 196, 29 missing ages), so let learners discover it before you explain.
Part 5 — Lists. The one data structure the tidyverse sessions never show, and the one learners hit first in real analyses: every test and model result is a list, and so is every Bioconductor object. Use the box analogy: [[ ]] takes the item out of the box, [ ] gives a smaller box. Show is.list(linelist) — the “aha” that a data frame is a list of columns explains $, [[ ]], and (in Session 8) why map() runs once per column. “Results are lists” (t.test()) is reading only: point to it on screen 2 and say that the statistics come later; the point is the shape of the result. Learners who want to try it have ⭐ Bonus 1.
Part 6 — Tidy data and pivot_longer(). Start from the diagram on screen 2: follow one orange box (a column name) into the symptom column and one blue box (a cell) into present. Point out that “observation” depends on the question: wide symptoms are fine for one symptom at a time, but long format lets one count() handle all five. nrow(symptoms_long) is 32255 = 6451 patients × 5 symptoms. The plot is reading only, a preview of Session 6: don’t explain ggplot yet.
Part 7 — pivot_wider(). Emphasize the rule of thumb: long for R, wide for people. Mention values_fill = 0 (the hospital × outcome table has no empty combinations, so it isn’t needed here).
Wrap-up. Today: vectors and types, c(), class(), vectorized maths and comparisons, sum()/mean() of TRUE/FALSE, [ ], $, [[ ]], lists and str(), test results as lists, tidy data, pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(). Next is Session 5 (Summarizing: count(), group_by() + summarise(), tabyl(), Table 1); Session 8 returns to vectors and subsetting when writing functions and loops.

title: Instructor notes: Session 6
text:
Teaching notes by part
Every part. Build each plot one layer at a time and run it after every +, so learners see what each layer adds.
Part 1 — Set up. Point out that the factor order from Session 5 isn’t saved in the .rds file, so it has to be set again right after importing — and that import() and mutate() can go in one pipeline.
Part 2 — The grammar of graphics. Run the three steps separately: empty canvas, axes only, then bars. Stress + not %>% between layers, and that + goes at the end of the line — the two most common beginner errors.
Part 3 — Histograms. Point out the “using bins = 30” message from the Part 2 plot, then choose binwidth yourself. Live-try binwidth = 1 and binwidth = 10 so learners see the shape change. In TRY IT 3, reassure learners that the “removed rows” warning is just the 29 missing ages.
Part 4 — Mapping vs setting. This is the key idea. Ask the class:

What happens if you put fill = "blue" inside aes()? Have them try it first. — The bars are pink-red and the legend says “blue”: ggplot treated “blue” as data (a column whose every value is the word “blue”) and gave it the first default color.

Part 5 — Scatter plots. With 6,451 rows, many points overlap — show size and alpha fixing that. When filtering inside the pipeline, point out the switch: %>% into ggplot(), then + between layers. In TRY IT 5, emphasize that a flat trend line (“no relationship”) is a result too.
Part 6 — Box plots. Walk through the parts of the box (median, IQR, whiskers at 1.5 × IQR, outliers). Ask the class:

Why is the mean (diamond) above the median (line)? — The ages are right-skewed: a few older patients pull the mean up (female: median 11, mean 12.7; male: median 17, mean 19.5).

Mention geom_violin() as an alternative.
Part 7 — Labels and themes. Point out that a complete theme like theme_minimal() resets everything, so it must come before theme(legend.position = ...). base_size = 14 is handy for slides. Early finishers: ⭐ BONUS (fill by vaccinated; geom_violin()).
Wrap-up. Today: ggplot(), aes(), geom_histogram(), geom_point(), geom_smooth(), geom_boxplot(), stat_summary(), labs(), themes. Next, Session 7 — Plotting further: bar charts, choosing colors, epidemic curves, facets, and saving plots to files.
