title: Instructor notes: Session 8
text:
Teaching notes by part
The motivating example. Keep returning to it: “Your manager wants an epidemic curve for every hospital, every week.” By the end, one loop does it.
Part 2 — Writing your first function. Show that a function only exists after you run the whole block — it then appears in the Variables pane. When you change a function, re-run the block, or R keeps using the old version. Point out that c_to_f() is vectorized because the maths inside is, so it works inside mutate(). The f_to_c(104.7) result (40.4) is the Fahrenheit temperature learners found in the measles data in Session 1.
Part 3 — Functions that use data. Point out that pct() replaces the round(mean(...) * 100, 1) learners wrote over and over in Session 5, and that paste("Weekly cases:", hospital) gives every plot the right title. In TRY IT 3, watch for learners naming the argument district: then filter(district == district) compares the column with itself and keeps every row — no error, just the wrong answer (n = 1163 instead of 342). That’s why the argument is called district_name. The lesson page has this as a warning box.
Part 4 — if / else. Run fever_status(c(39.2, 36.9)) live so learners see the error “the condition has length > 1”: if asks one yes/no question. Then switch to the vectorized if_else() from Session 2. Present stop() input checks as where if really shines. (Both error chunks are deliberate; the lesson page shows the errors.)
Part 5 — for loops. Stress that inside a loop nothing prints automatically (print()), and that results need a container created before the loop. In the payoff loop, point out make_clean_names() turning “St. Mark’s Maternity Hospital” into st_marks_maternity_hospital and paste0() building the file name: six files, one loop — and next week you just re-run it. Have learners check the Explorer for the new files in outputs/. Remind them that mutate(), group_by() + summarise(), and across() already loop for them; a for loop is for repeating a whole task.
Part 6 — map() and walk(). Point out that a data frame is a list of columns, so map_dbl() runs once per column, and that ~ .x is the same shorthand they used with across() in Session 3. Loop or map()? Both are fine — tell learners to use the one they can read.
🔁 lapply() / sapply() (4 min). Learners who go on to bioinformatics will meet these constantly: Bioconductor code and vignettes use the apply family far more than purrr. Show the translation table, then let the class predict what sapply(three_cols, range, na.rm = TRUE) returns before running it: the matrix is the teaching moment for why map_dbl() exists.
Wrap-up. Today: function(), arguments and defaults, if/else, stop(), if_else(), for loops, map(), map_dbl(), walk(). The big idea: write it once, run it many times — a function plus a loop (or walk()) turns an hour of copy-paste into one line you can re-run every week. Where to go next: R for Data Science (functions and iteration chapters) and The Epidemiologist R Handbook.

Note🔍 What this code does




filter(age_unit == "months") keeps only the rows where age_unit is exactly “months”. == asks “is it equal?” for every row, and filter() keeps the rows where the answer is TRUE. nrow() then counts them: 37.
arrange(desc(ht_cm)) sorts by height, tallest first. The top heights, 295, 287, and 272 cm, are impossible. They’re on the problem list.

== equal · != not equal · > < >= <= · %in% c(...) one of several values · is.na() missing · & and · | or
Use == (two equals signs) to compare. One = is for naming arguments.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Longer pipelines
Put each step on its own line, with the %>% at the end of the line. select() keeps only the columns you name:

👀 Follow along 2.3 — A longer pipeline, one step per line: select() Case ID, wt_kg, and ht_cm, then arrange() by wt_kg, then head(5).


linelist_raw %>%
  select(`Case ID`, wt_kg, ht_cm) %>%   # keep three columns
  arrange(wt_kg) %>%                    # sort by weight
  head(5)                               # show the first 5 rows

  Case ID wt_kg ht_cm
1  6056ba   -11    24
2  6056ba   -11    24
3  7400b3   -10    13
4  0fde59   -10    18
5  fca629    -9    24








Note🔍 What this code does




select(`Case ID`, wt_kg, ht_cm) keeps only these three columns, in this order. Case ID has a space in it, so it needs backticks.
arrange(wt_kg) sorts the rows by weight, smallest first, and head(5) keeps the first 5.
Each line ends with %>%, so R knows the next line continues the same pipeline. The text after # is a comment for people; R ignores it.
Without the pipe, you’d have to put each function inside the next one: head(arrange(select(linelist_raw, ...), wt_kg), 5), which you read from the inside out. The pipe keeps the steps in the order they happen.









Note



You may also see |>, the pipe built into R itself. For this workshop they do the same thing.








WarningCommon mistakes




Put %>% at the end of a line, not at the start of the next one. R stops at a complete line, so a line starting with %>% gives an error.
Don’t end the last line with %>%: R then waits for another step (a + appears in the Console). Press Esc and remove it.

These are the Fahrenheit temperatures you found with skim() in Session 1: 27 of them. You’ll convert them in Part 5. From here on, almost every piece of code in the workshop uses the pipe.











Note📖 Good to know




Most tidyverse functions take the data as their first argument. That’s what makes the pipe work: whatever comes out of one step goes straight into the first argument of the next.
The pipe %>% comes from the magrittr package, which the tidyverse loads for you.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
clean_names()
One function (from janitor) makes every name lower case, replaces spaces and dots with _, and removes symbols. "Case ID" becomes case_id — after this, you never need backticks again!

👀 Follow along 3.1 — Create linelist_clean from linelist_raw with clean_names(). Compare names() before and after.
Pattern: NEW_DATA <- OLD_DATA %>% clean_names()


names(linelist_raw)

 [1] "Case ID"         "infection date"  "date.onset"      "hosp date"      
 [5] "date of outcome" "OUTCOME"         "Gender"          "hospital"       
 [9] "age"             "age_unit"        "wt_kg"           "ht_cm"          

linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>%
  clean_names()

names(linelist_clean)

 [1] "case_id"         "infection_date"  "date_onset"      "hosp_date"      
 [5] "date_of_outcome" "outcome"         "gender"          "hospital"       
 [9] "age"             "age_unit"        "wt_kg"           "ht_cm"          








Note🔍 What this code does




The first names() shows the 12 original names, as in Session 1.
linelist_raw %>% clean_names() makes a copy of the data with tidied names, and linelist_clean <- saves it as a new object. linelist_raw is unchanged.
The second names() shows the result: "Case ID" became case_id, "date.onset" became date_onset, and "OUTCOME" became outcome. Only the names change; the data in the columns stays the same.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
rename()
rename(new_name = old_name) — the new name goes on the left.

👀 Follow along 3.2 — Rename infection_date → date_of_infection, date_onset → onset_date, and hosp_date → hospital_date.
Pattern: DATA <- DATA %>% rename(NEW_NAME = OLD_NAME, NEW_NAME = OLD_NAME)


linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  rename(
    date_of_infection = infection_date,
    onset_date        = date_onset,
    hospital_date     = hosp_date
  )

names(linelist_clean)

 [1] "case_id"           "date_of_infection" "onset_date"       
 [4] "hospital_date"     "date_of_outcome"   "outcome"          
 [7] "gender"            "hospital"          "age"              
[10] "age_unit"          "wt_kg"             "ht_cm"            








Note🔍 What this code does




rename() changes three names. In each pair, the new name is on the left of = and the current name on the right.
All other columns keep their names, and there are still 12 columns.
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>% ... takes the current version, changes it, and saves it back under the same name.









TipOne step at a time



We build the clean data step by step. Each step takes the current version, changes one thing, and saves it back with <-:
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>% STEP()
If your object gets into a bad state, re-run from the first step (linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>% clean_names()). In Part 8 we put all the steps into one pipeline.








Important✏️ TRY IT 3 (2 min): clean the measles column names



Create measles_clean from measles_raw with clean_names(). What did `Temp (C)` and `Vaccinated?` turn into?
✅ Check: names(measles_clean) includes "temp_c" and "vaccinated"






NoteShow solution






measles_clean <- measles_raw %>%
  clean_names()

names(measles_clean)

 [1] "patient_id"       "report_date"      "district"         "sex"             
 [5] "age_years"        "vaccinated"       "fever"            "rash"            
 [9] "temp_c"           "days_in_hospital" "outcome"         


`Temp (C)` became temp_c and `Vaccinated?` became vaccinated: the parentheses and the ? are removed, and the space becomes _.











Note📖 Good to know




The names clean_names() makes are in snake_case: lower case, with words joined by _. Most R code uses this style, and you never need backticks for it.
clean_names() also makes repeated names unique (a second a becomes a_2) and puts an x in front of names that start with a number (2020 cases becomes x2020_cases), because R names can’t start with a number.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Dates
as.Date() converts text or date-times to dates.

👀 Follow along 4.1 — Turn date_of_infection, onset_date, hospital_date, and date_of_outcome into dates with as.Date().
Pattern: DATA <- DATA %>% mutate(COLUMN = as.Date(COLUMN), COLUMN = as.Date(COLUMN))


linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(
    date_of_infection = as.Date(date_of_infection),
    onset_date        = as.Date(onset_date),
    hospital_date     = as.Date(hospital_date),
    date_of_outcome   = as.Date(date_of_outcome)
  )

linelist_clean %>% select(date_of_infection:date_of_outcome) %>% glimpse()

Rows: 6,604
Columns: 4
$ date_of_infection <date> 2014-05-08, NA, NA, 2014-05-04, 2014-05-18, 2014-05…
$ onset_date        <date> 2014-05-13, 2014-05-13, 2014-05-16, 2014-05-18, 201…
$ hospital_date     <date> 2014-05-15, 2014-05-14, 2014-05-18, 2014-05-20, 201…
$ date_of_outcome   <date> NA, 2014-05-18, 2014-05-30, NA, 2014-05-29, 2014-05…








Note🔍 What this code does




Inside mutate(), each line column = as.Date(column) overwrites one column with a date version of itself. Four columns are converted in one mutate(), separated by commas.
onset_date was text ("2014-05-13") and the other three were date-times from Excel. as.Date() turns both kinds into plain dates.
select(date_of_infection:date_of_outcome) uses : to pick every column from date_of_infection to date_of_outcome. glimpse() then shows that all four are now <date>.
Missing dates stay missing (NA).









NoteDates written in other formats



as.Date() expects year-month-day ("2014-05-13"). For other formats, the lubridate package (part of the tidyverse) has functions named after the order: dmy("13/05/2014"), mdy("05/13/2014"), ymd("2014-05-13").

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Numbers stored as text
as.numeric() turns text like "56" into the number 56. Text that isn’t a number (like "unknown") becomes NA, and R warns you: “NAs introduced by coercion”. That warning is fine if you expected it.

👀 Follow along 4.2 — Turn age into a number with as.numeric().


linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age = as.numeric(age))

class(linelist_clean$age)

[1] "numeric"








Note🔍 What this code does




mutate(age = as.numeric(age)) replaces the text column age with numbers.
class() tells you what kind of values a column holds: now "numeric".
There’s no warning here, because every filled-in age was a number written as text. The 100 ages that were already missing stay NA. In the measles data (TRY IT 4), “unknown” can’t become a number, so you will see the warning there.









WarningCommon mistakes




Forgetting the <- at the start: the result prints in the Console but isn’t saved.









Important✏️ TRY IT 4 (3 min): fix the measles types



In measles_clean:

make report_date a date with as.Date()
make age_years a number with as.numeric(). Which values became NA?

✅ Check: summary(measles_clean$age_years) shows a maximum of 999. Suspicious!






NoteShow solution






measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    report_date = as.Date(report_date),
    age_years   = as.numeric(age_years)   # "unknown" becomes NA (the warning is expected)
  )

summary(measles_clean$age_years)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
   0.00    4.00    7.00   12.13   12.00  999.00      27 


The 27 "unknown" ages became NA — that is what the warning is about. A maximum age of 999 is not a real age; we fix it in the next part.











Note📖 Good to know




R stores a date as the number of days since 1 January 1970: 13 May 2014 is day 16203. That’s what lets you subtract dates or sort them. You’ll see these numbers in Part 5 when something goes wrong.
as.Date(), as.numeric(), and as.character() all follow the same pattern: as. plus the type you want.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Ages in months → years
“If the unit is months, divide by 12; otherwise keep the age.”

👀 Follow along 5.1 — Create age_years (ages in months divided by 12).


linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age_years = if_else(age_unit == "months", age / 12, age))

linelist_clean %>%
  filter(age_unit == "months") %>%
  select(age, age_unit, age_years) %>%
  head()

  age age_unit age_years
1  24   months 2.0000000
2  NA   months        NA
3   7   months 0.5833333
4   7   months 0.5833333
5  24   months 2.0000000
6  24   months 2.0000000








Tip🧩 Reading a function call



Most cleaning steps in this workshop have the same shape as the code you just ran:
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>% mutate(age_years = if_else(age_unit == "months", age / 12, age))








Piece
What it is
What it does




linelist_clean <-
the object and the assignment arrow
saves the result back under the same name


linelist_clean %>%
the data and the pipe
passes the data into the next function


mutate(...)
a function from dplyr (tidyverse)
adds or changes a column


age_years =
a named argument of mutate()
the name of the new column


if_else(...)
a function used as the value of that column
works out a value for every row


age_unit == "months"
the first argument of if_else(): a condition
TRUE or FALSE for each row


age / 12
the second argument
used where the condition is TRUE


age
the third argument
used where the condition is FALSE



R works it out from the inside out: for every row, if_else() checks the condition and picks age / 12 or age; mutate() puts the results in the new column age_years; and <- saves the changed data as linelist_clean.








Note🔍 What this code does




if_else() checks every row: if age_unit is "months", the new age_years is age / 12; otherwise it’s age, unchanged.
The second pipeline only checks the result and isn’t saved: it keeps the rows in months, shows three columns, and prints the first 6.
24 months became 2 years and 7 months became 0.58 years. One of these patients has no age (NA), and it stays NA: missing in, missing out.









Note🤔 Think about it: what would have happened in later analyses if we had skipped this step?





A 6-month-old baby would be counted as 6 years old. All 37 ages recorded in months would be too old, which would shift the age groups and the average age.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Impossible values → missing
Weights of zero or below are impossible. Instead of deleting the whole row (and losing the patient’s age, outcome, and dates), we replace only the bad value with NA.

👀 Follow along 5.2 — Replace weights of 0 or below with NA.


linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(wt_kg = if_else(wt_kg <= 0, NA, wt_kg))

summary(linelist_clean$wt_kg)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
   1.00   41.00   55.00   52.99   66.00  111.00      34 








Note🔍 What this code does




wt_kg <= 0 is TRUE for the 34 weights that are zero or below. For those, if_else() puts NA; every other weight is kept as it was.
summary() now shows a smallest weight of 1 kg and 34 NAs. The rows are still there, with all their other information.









Note🔁 The base R way: ifelse() (one letter shorter, one big difference)



Base R has ifelse(), and you will see it everywhere. It works the same way until you use it on dates. Say we want an “estimated onset” that uses the hospital date when the onset date is missing. Compare the first 3 values (reading only, you don’t need to type this):

if_else(is.na(linelist_clean$onset_date), linelist_clean$hospital_date, linelist_clean$onset_date) %>% head(3)

[1] "2014-05-13" "2014-05-13" "2014-05-16"

ifelse(is.na(linelist_clean$onset_date), linelist_clean$hospital_date, linelist_clean$onset_date) %>% head(3)

[1] 16203 16203 16206








Note🔍 What this code does




is.na(linelist_clean$onset_date) is TRUE where the onset date is missing. Then the hospital date is used; otherwise the onset date.
This code runs outside mutate(), so each column is pulled out with $.
Both lines pick the same values. if_else() prints them as dates ("2014-05-13"); ifelse() prints 16203, the same date as a number of days since 1 January 1970.



ifelse() silently turned the dates into numbers (days since 1 January 1970). if_else() keeps the type, and gives an error instead of a surprise when the two values have different types. That strictness is why we use if_else() in this workshop.








Important✏️ TRY IT 5 (4 min): 999 and Fahrenheit



In measles_clean:

999 is a code for “unknown”: replace age_years of 999 with NA
temperatures above 45 were entered in Fahrenheit. Convert them: Celsius = (Fahrenheit − 32) × 5 / 9, rounded to 1 decimal with round(..., 1)

✅ Check: summary() shows age_years max 52 and temp_c max 40.9






NoteShow solution






measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    age_years = if_else(age_years == 999, NA, age_years),
    temp_c    = if_else(temp_c > 45, round((temp_c - 32) * 5 / 9, 1), temp_c)
  )

summary(measles_clean$age_years)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   8.796  12.000  52.000      31 

summary(measles_clean$temp_c)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  36.00   38.40   38.90   38.82   39.40   40.90 


The four 999s are now NA (31 missing ages in total), and the 27 Fahrenheit temperatures are now in °C, so every temperature is between 36 and 40.9.











Note📖 Good to know




Two shortcuts for jobs you just did with if_else(): na_if(age_years, 999) turns every 999 into NA, and coalesce(onset_date, hospital_date) takes the onset date, or the hospital date when the onset date is missing (the “estimated onset” from the 🔁 box). Both give the same result as the if_else() versions.
A comparison with a missing value gives a missing answer: NA <= 0 is NA, not TRUE or FALSE. So if_else() gives NA for those rows, and missing values stay missing unless you deal with them on purpose (Session 3).
Prefer NA to deleting rows. A patient with an impossible weight still has a real age, outcome, and dates that you want to keep.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Gender

👀 Follow along 6.1 — Recode gender "m" → "male" and "f" → "female". Check with count().


linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(gender = case_when(
    gender == "m" ~ "male",
    gender == "f" ~ "female"
  ))

linelist_clean %>% count(gender)

  gender    n
1 female 3140
2   male 3147
3   <NA>  317








Note🔍 What this code does




case_when() checks each line in order: rows where gender is "m" get "male", rows where it’s "f" get "female".
The result overwrites the gender column. count(gender) checks it: 3140 female, 3147 male, and 317 NA.
The 317 missing values matched neither line, and there’s no .default, so they stay NA.



Any row that matches no condition becomes NA — here, that is the rows that were already missing.

Hospital names (using the look-up table)

hosp_info

str_detect(column, "pattern") is TRUE when the text contains the pattern, so one line catches every misspelling. | means “or”.

linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(hospital_name = case_when(
    str_detect(hospital, "Central")           ~ "Central Hospital",
    str_detect(hospital, "Military|Mitylira") ~ "Military Hospital",

linelist_clean %>% count(hospital, hospital_name)

                               hospital                 hospital_name    n
1                       Central Hopital              Central Hospital   11
2                      Central Hospital              Central Hospital  457
3                            HMO Health                    HMO Health  288

Note🔍 What this code does




hosp_info lists the 6 correct hospital names. count(hospital) shows 14 different values in the linelist, including misspellings and NA.
Each str_detect(hospital, "...") line is TRUE when the hospital name contains that piece of text, so "Central" catches both “Central Hospital” and “Central Hopital”. "Military|Mitylira" catches either spelling.
The result goes into a new column, hospital_name; the original hospital column stays as it was, so you can compare the two.
.default = "Other/Unknown" catches everything else: the hospital called “Other” and the missing values.
count(hospital, hospital_name) lists every old value next to its new one (14 rows), so you can check that each spelling landed in the right place.









NoteOther useful text functions (stringr)



str_to_lower(), str_to_upper(), str_to_title() change capitalization (str_to_title("north") gives "North") · str_trim() removes extra spaces · str_replace(x, "old", "new") replaces text. You may need these for the TRY ITs!
To check for any of several exact values, use %in%: sex %in% c("Male", "male", "M").








WarningCommon mistakes




Use ~ (tilde), not =, between the condition and the new value
Put a comma after each line except the last
Check every recode with count(old_column, new_column)









Important✏️ TRY IT 6 (4 min): sex and vaccinated



In measles_clean, recode

sex: Male / male / M → "male", Female / female / F → "female"
vaccinated: Yes / yes / Y → "Yes", No / no / N / NO → "No", Unknown → "Unknown"

Pattern: COLUMN %in% c("VALUE_1", "VALUE_2") ~ "NEW_VALUE"
✅ Check: count(sex) shows female 533, male 642, NA 40; count(vaccinated) shows only No, Unknown, Yes






NoteShow solution






measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      sex %in% c("Male", "male", "M")     ~ "male",
      sex %in% c("Female", "female", "F") ~ "female"
    ),
    vaccinated = case_when(
      vaccinated %in% c("Yes", "yes", "Y")     ~ "Yes",
      vaccinated %in% c("No", "no", "N", "NO") ~ "No",
      vaccinated == "Unknown"                  ~ "Unknown"
    )
  )

measles_clean %>% count(sex)

     sex   n
1 female 533
2   male 642
3   <NA>  40

measles_clean %>% count(vaccinated)

  vaccinated   n
1         No 741
2    Unknown 183
3        Yes 291


Six spellings of sex became two values (the 40 missing stay NA), and eight spellings of vaccinated became three: No 741, Unknown 183, Yes 291.











Note🤔 Think about it: it ran without an error, but is it right?





Say you forgot "M" in the male line: sex %in% c("Male", "male") ~ "male". What happens?
R gives no error and no warning. The 86 patients recorded as "M" match no line, so they quietly become NA: count(sex) shows male 556 and NA 126 instead of male 642 and NA 40. The only way to notice is to check, for example with count(old_column, new_column) or by comparing the number of NAs before and after. Code that runs is not the same as code that’s right.









Important✏️ TRY IT 7 (5 min, homework if behind): district



Make district one of North, South, East, West, Central.
If you run out of time in class, finish this at home, then run your TRY IT 9 line again so the saved file has the clean districts. Session 3 joins on district.

Step 1: district = str_to_title(district) fixes the capitals
Step 2: case_when() + str_detect() fixes the misspellings (“Nroth”, “Cetnral”) and the “… District” versions. Keep NA as NA (no .default).

✅ Check: count(district) shows exactly 5 districts plus NA (34)






NoteShow solution






measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    district = str_to_title(district),
    district = case_when(
      str_detect(district, "North|Nroth")     ~ "North",
      str_detect(district, "South")           ~ "South",
      str_detect(district, "East")            ~ "East",
      str_detect(district, "West")            ~ "West",
      str_detect(district, "Central|Cetnral") ~ "Central"
    )
  )

measles_clean %>% count(district)

  district   n
1  Central 113
2     East 233
3    North 356
4    South 297
5     West 182
6     <NA>  34


str_to_title() turns “north” into “North” first, so each str_detect() line only has to catch the misspellings and the “… District” versions. Because there is no .default, the 34 missing districts stay NA.











Note📖 Good to know




str_detect() is case-sensitive: "north" does not contain "North". That’s why TRY IT 7 runs str_to_title() first.
All the stringr text functions start with str_. In Positron, type str_ and the list of them pops up.
The order of the lines in case_when() matters. If a value could match two lines, it gets the first one.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
BMI
mutate() can calculate a new column from other columns. Here is BMI, calculated from weight and height, then cleaned (reading only, you don’t need to type this: BMI is included in the Part 8 pipeline).

linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(bmi = round(wt_kg / (ht_cm / 100)^2, 1))

summary(linelist_clean$bmi)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  10.90   24.60   32.10   48.09   49.88 1250.00      34 








Note🤔 Think about it: a BMI of 1,250?





That is impossible: the heights and weights don’t fit together. Set BMIs outside a plausible range (10–60) to NA.




linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(bmi = if_else(bmi < 10 | bmi > 60, NA, bmi))

summary(linelist_clean$bmi)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  10.90   23.20   28.70   30.58   36.50   60.00    1382 








Note🔍 What this code does




BMI is weight in kg divided by height in metres, squared. ht_cm / 100 turns centimetres into metres, ^2 squares it, and round(..., 1) keeps one decimal.
The first summary() shows a maximum BMI of 1250 and 34 NAs: the weights you set to NA in Part 5 give a missing BMI.
In the second block, bmi < 10 | bmi > 60 is TRUE when the BMI is below 10 or above 60. Those 1348 values become NA, so 1382 BMIs are missing in total, and the rest lie between 10.9 and 60.



About 1,400 BMIs are now NA, because many height and weight values in this teaching dataset are unrealistic. Setting only the bad value to NA (instead of filtering out those rows) keeps everything else we know about each patient.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Age groups

👀 Follow along 7.1 — Create age_cat: Under 18, 18-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, 70-79, 80+.


linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age_cat = case_when(
    age_years < 18 ~ "Under 18",
    age_years < 30 ~ "18-29",
    age_years < 40 ~ "30-39",
    age_years < 50 ~ "40-49",
    age_years < 60 ~ "50-59",
    age_years < 70 ~ "60-69",
    age_years < 80 ~ "70-79",
    age_years >= 80 ~ "80+"
  ))

linelist_clean %>% count(age_cat)

   age_cat    n
1    18-29 1487
2    30-39  598
3    40-49  252
4    50-59   78
5    60-69   27
6    70-79    6
7      80+    1
8 Under 18 4055
9     <NA>  100








Note🔍 What this code does




Each line checks one upper limit. A patient aged 25 fails age_years < 18, passes age_years < 30, and gets “18-29”. case_when() stops at the first TRUE line.
The last line, age_years >= 80, is written out in full so that missing ages match no line and stay NA.
count(age_cat) shows most patients are children: 4055 are under 18. The 100 patients with no age are NA.



Because case_when() stops at the first TRUE line, age_years < 30 only catches ages 18–29 (younger ages were already caught by the line above).
count() lists the groups in alphabetical order (“18-29” before “Under 18”). In Session 5 you will learn how to put them in a sensible order with factors.






Note🔁 The base R way: cut()



Base R’s cut() makes groups from numbers by giving the break points. right = FALSE means each group includes its lower limit (18 goes into “18-29”). Here are the same groups, counted with table(useNA = "ifany") (reading only):

cut(linelist_clean$age_years,
    breaks = c(0, 18, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, Inf),
    labels = c("Under 18", "18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80+"),
    right  = FALSE) %>%
  table(useNA = "ifany")

.
Under 18    18-29    30-39    40-49    50-59    60-69    70-79      80+ 
    4055     1487      598      252       78       27        6        1 
    <NA> 
     100 








Note🔍 What this code does




breaks gives the edges of the groups: 0, 18, 30, … and Inf (infinity), so there’s no upper limit for the last group.
labels names the 8 groups, in order. There is always one label fewer than there are breaks.
right = FALSE puts each break into the group above it, so 18 goes into “18-29”.
The result is piped into table(useNA = "ifany"), which counts each group, including the missing ages.



The same counts as case_when(), and already in the right order, because cut() returns a factor (Session 5). Forgetting right = FALSE is the classic mistake: then an 18-year-old lands in “Under 18”.








WarningCommon mistakes



Ending with TRUE ~ "80+" (or .default = "80+") puts every patient with a missing age into the 80+ group. Write the last condition out in full (age_years >= 80 ~ "80+") so missing ages stay NA.








Important✏️ TRY IT 8 (4 min): outcome and age groups



In measles_clean:

make outcome consistent with str_to_title()
create age_cat: “Under 5”, “5-9”, “10-14”, “15+”

✅ Check: count(outcome) shows only Died, Recovered, NA; count(age_cat) shows 4 groups plus NA (31)






NoteShow solution






measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    outcome = str_to_title(outcome),
    age_cat = case_when(
      age_years < 5   ~ "Under 5",
      age_years < 10  ~ "5-9",
      age_years < 15  ~ "10-14",
      age_years >= 15 ~ "15+"
    )
  )

measles_clean %>% count(outcome)

    outcome    n
1      Died   52
2 Recovered 1095
3      <NA>   68

measles_clean %>% count(age_cat)

  age_cat   n
1   10-14 232
2     15+ 205
3     5-9 368
4 Under 5 379
5    <NA>  31


“died” and “recovered” now match “Died” and “Recovered” (52 died, 1095 recovered, 68 missing). The 31 missing ages (the 27 “unknown” plus the four 999s) stay NA because the last condition is written out in full.











Note📖 Good to know




R follows the usual maths order: brackets first, then ^, then * and /, then + and -. So wt_kg / (ht_cm / 100)^2 divides the weight by the squared height.
| means “or” and & means “and”. You can combine as many conditions as you need.

Save your work
export() is the opposite of import(). Save cleaned data to processed_data/ — never over the raw file.

👀 Follow along 8.2 — Save linelist_clean as processed_data/linelist_clean.rds.
Pattern: export(DATA, here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.rds"))


export(linelist_clean, here("processed_data", "linelist_clean.rds"))







Note🔍 What this code does




export() takes the data first, then the path to save it to. Like import(), it picks the file type from the ending: .rds here.
Nothing prints. The file appears in the processed_data/ folder in the Explorer.
If a file with that name already exists (like the ready-made copy), export() replaces it without asking.



.rds is R’s own file format. It keeps everything exactly as it is in R — dates stay dates and missing values stay NA — so it’s the best choice for a file you will open in R again. (We compare .rds and .csv in Session 3.)
Session 3 starts from this file.

Brought your own data? Fix the problems on your own problem list, then export() the clean version to processed_data/.









Note📖 Good to know




Keeping the whole cleaning in one script means anyone can see every change you made to the data, and rerun it if the raw data is updated.
Use .rds for files you’ll open in R again, and .csv or .xlsx for sharing with people who use Excel. export() makes any of them: just change the ending.

text:
One type per vector
If you mix types, R converts everything to the most flexible type — usually text. This is why a few “unknown” values turned the measles Age (years) column into text in Session 1:

👀 Follow along 2.3 — What happens with c(1, 2, "unknown") and c(1, TRUE, FALSE)?


c(1, 2, "unknown")

[1] "1"       "2"       "unknown"

c(1, TRUE, FALSE)    # TRUE becomes 1, FALSE becomes 0

[1] 1 1 0








Note🔍 What this code does




c(1, 2, "unknown") mixes numbers and text, so R turns the numbers into text: "1" "2" "unknown". The quotes in the output show they’re text now, and you can no longer calculate with them.
c(1, TRUE, FALSE) mixes numbers and TRUE/FALSE. Numbers are the more flexible type, so TRUE becomes 1 and FALSE becomes 0: 1 1 0.
From least to most flexible: logical (TRUE/FALSE), then numeric, then character. R always picks the most flexible type in the vector.

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Lists, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
Missing values spread
Any calculation with NA gives NA, unless you tell R to skip them:

👀 Follow along 2.4 — mean(c(38, 39, NA)) with and without na.rm = TRUE.


mean(c(38, 39, NA))

[1] NA

mean(c(38, 39, NA), na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 38.5








Note🔍 What this code does




mean(c(38, 39, NA)) gives NA. One value is unknown, so the mean is unknown too: R tells you instead of guessing.
na.rm = TRUE (“NA remove”) tells mean() to skip the missing values: the mean of 38 and 39 is 38.5.
The same argument works in sum(), min(), max(), median(), and sd().









Important✏️ TRY IT 2 (3 min): types in the measles data



Use class() on measles$age_years, measles$vaccinated, and measles$report_date, and length() on measles$temp_c.
✅ Check: “numeric”, “character”, “Date”, and 1163






NoteShow solution






class(measles$age_years)

[1] "numeric"

class(measles$vaccinated)

[1] "character"

class(measles$report_date)

[1] "Date"

length(measles$temp_c)

[1] 1163


Ages are numbers, vaccination status is text, and the report date is a real date. The length is 1163 — one value per row, because a column is just a vector.











Note📖 Good to know




NA and “Unknown” are different. NA means the value is missing, and R treats it specially: calculations with it give NA. “Unknown” is ordinary text, which R counts like any other value. In this data, unknown symptoms are written “Unknown”, so fever has no NAs.
str() describes any object: its type, its size, and its first values. For a data frame it works like glimpse().
Don’t test for missing values with == NA. ages == NA asks “is this age equal to an unknown value?”, and the answer is always unknown: NA for every row, so sum(ages == NA) is NA. Use is.na(ages) instead: sum(is.na(ages)) gives 96.
IDs with leading zeros should stay text. as.numeric("00123") gives 123: the zeros are gone, and the ID no longer matches the same ID in another dataset. Store IDs, ZIP codes, and phone numbers as text, even when they look like numbers.

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Lists, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
Comparisons are vectorized too
A comparison gives a logical vector, one TRUE/FALSE per element:

👀 Follow along 3.3 — temps_c > 38, then sum() and mean() of linelist$temp > 38, and mean(linelist$fever == "yes") (the next two code blocks).


temps_c > 38

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE


TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, so:

sum() of a comparison counts the TRUEs
mean() of a comparison gives the proportion that are TRUE


sum(linelist$temp > 38, na.rm = TRUE)    # how many patients had temp above 38

[1] 4943

mean(linelist$temp > 38, na.rm = TRUE)   # what proportion

[1] 0.7846032

mean(linelist$fever == "yes")            # proportion with fever

[1] 0.7870098








Note🔍 What this code does




temps_c > 38 compares each value with 38 and gives one TRUE or FALSE per value: FALSE TRUE TRUE.
sum(linelist$temp > 38, na.rm = TRUE) counts the TRUEs: 4943 patients had a temperature above 38 °C. na.rm = TRUE skips the 151 patients with no temperature.
mean() of the same comparison gives the proportion: 0.785, so about 78% of the patients with a recorded temperature had one above 38 °C.
mean(linelist$fever == "yes") is the proportion of all patients with fever: 0.787. fever has no missing values (unknowns are written “Unknown”), so no na.rm is needed.



You will use this trick again in Session 5: mean(fever == "yes") * 100 inside summarise() gives the percentage with fever in each group.






Important✏️ TRY IT 3 (4 min): vectorized calculations




Convert measles$temp_c to Fahrenheit and look at the first values with head()
Count the cases with a temperature of 39 or more: sum(... >= 39)
Find the proportion of cases who were vaccinated: mean(... == "Yes")

✅ Check: a) starts 100.94, 101.12 b) 565 c) 0.238






NoteShow solution






head(measles$temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32)    # a)

[1] 100.94 101.12 102.74 100.40 102.02 101.30

sum(measles$temp_c >= 39)            # b)

[1] 565

mean(measles$vaccinated == "Yes")    # c)

[1] 0.2381771


565 cases had a temperature of 39 °C or more, and 23.8% of cases were vaccinated. No na.rm = TRUE is needed here because temp_c has no missing values after cleaning.











Note📖 Good to know




Why no loop? In many programming languages you’d write a loop to go through the values one at a time. In R, vectorized code is shorter and much faster, because the loop runs inside R’s own built-in code. Loops still have their uses (Session 8).
The functions you used in Session 2, such as as.Date(), if_else(), case_when(), and str_detect(), are vectorized too. That’s why they worked on whole columns.

temps_c[1]            # first element

[1] 36.8

temps_c[c(1, 3)]      # first and third

[1] 36.8 40.1

temps_c[-1]           # everything EXCEPT the first

[1] 38.5 40.1

temps_c[temps_c > 38] # elements that meet a condition

[1] 38.5 40.1








Note🔍 What this code does




temps_c[1] gives the first value, 36.8. Positions in R start at 1.
temps_c[c(1, 3)] gives the first and third values: 36.8 and 40.1.
temps_c[-1] drops the first value: 38.5 and 40.1.
In temps_c[temps_c > 38], the comparison inside the brackets gives FALSE TRUE TRUE, and the brackets keep the values where it’s TRUE: 38.5 and 40.1.

Data frames: df[rows, columns]
Inside the brackets, rows come first, then columns, separated by a comma. Leave one side empty to keep everything:

👀 Follow along 4.2 — linelist[1:3, c("case_id", "age_years", "outcome")] (the next two code blocks).


linelist[1:3, c("case_id", "age_years", "outcome")]   # rows 1–3, three columns

  case_id age_years outcome
1  5fe599         2 Unknown
2  8689b7         3 Recover
3  11f8ea        56 Recover



linelist[1:3, ]                                       # rows 1–3, all columns
linelist[, "age_years"]                               # all rows, one column







Note🔍 What this code does




In linelist[1:3, c("case_id", "age_years", "outcome")], the part before the comma chooses rows (1:3 means rows 1, 2, and 3) and the part after it chooses columns, by name.
1:3 is short for c(1, 2, 3).
In the second block, an empty side keeps everything: linelist[1:3, ] is rows 1–3 with all 19 columns, and linelist[, "age_years"] is every row of one column.

One column: $ and [[ ]]

👀 Follow along 4.3 — The first three hospital names with $ and with [[ ]].


linelist$hospital_name[1:3]        # $ with a name you type

[1] "Other/Unknown"                 "Other/Unknown"                
[3] "St. Mark's Maternity Hospital"

linelist[["hospital_name"]][1:3]   # [[ ]] with a name in quotes — useful inside functions

[1] "Other/Unknown"                 "Other/Unknown"                
[3] "St. Mark's Maternity Hospital"








Note🔍 What this code does




linelist$hospital_name and linelist[["hospital_name"]] both pull out the whole column as a vector, and [1:3] then keeps its first three values.
With $ you type the name itself. [[ ]] takes the name as text, so the name can also come from an object: col <- "hospital_name" and then linelist[[col]]. That’s why [[ ]] is the one to use inside your own functions (Session 8).

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Lists, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
Conditions
A condition inside [ ] keeps only the values where it is TRUE. For example, the mean temperature of patients who died (reading only, you don’t need to type this):

# Mean temperature of patients who died
mean(linelist$temp[linelist$outcome == "Death"], na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 38.59154








Note🔍 What this code does




linelist$outcome == "Death" gives TRUE for every patient who died.
linelist$temp[...] keeps the temperatures where that is TRUE: the temperatures of the patients who died.
mean(..., na.rm = TRUE) averages them, skipping missing temperatures: 38.6 °C. In Session 5 you’ll do the same with filter() and summarise().









WarningBase R and missing values



Read this box carefully: you’ll meet the same trap in TRY IT 4. Compare base R with filter() (reading only):

nrow(linelist[linelist$temp > 40, ])   # 244 rows?!

[1] 244

nrow(filter(linelist, temp > 40))     # 93 rows

[1] 93


Base R returns an extra row of NAs for every missing temperature (151 of them). filter() drops rows where the condition is NA. With base R, add & !is.na(temp), or just use filter():

nrow(linelist[linelist$temp > 40 & !is.na(linelist$temp), ])   # 93: fixed

[1] 93








Note🔍 What this code does




linelist$temp > 40 is NA for the 151 patients with no temperature. Inside [ ], each NA becomes a row filled with NAs, so base R returns 244 rows (93 + 151) instead of 93.
filter() keeps only the rows where the condition is TRUE, so it drops the NAs and returns 93.
& !is.na(linelist$temp) adds a second condition, “and the temperature isn’t missing”, which turns those NAs into FALSE.

Base R vs tidyverse








Task
Base R
Tidyverse




Rows that meet a condition
df[df$age > 40, ]
filter(df, age > 40)


Some columns
df[, c("a", "b")]
select(df, a, b)

df$a or df[["a"]]
pull(df, a)


First rows
df[1:5, ]
slice(df, 1:5) or head(df, 5)









WarningCommon mistakes




Forgetting the comma: df[1:3] picks columns 1–3, not rows!
Base R adds a row of NAs for every NA in the condition (see the box above). Add & !is.na(...), or use filter().









Important✏️ TRY IT 4 (5 min): subsetting the measles data



With base R,

Show rows 1–5 of the patient_id and temp_c columns of measles
Find the mean temperature of children who died (outcome == "Died")
Count the cases aged 15 or older with nrow(measles[...]), then with filter(). Why are the answers different? Fix the base R version.

✅ Check: a) the first ID is MS-0931 b) 38.75 c) 225 vs 196 (29 missing ages)






NoteShow solution






# a)
measles[1:5, c("patient_id", "temp_c")]

  patient_id temp_c
1    MS-0931   38.3
2    MS-0113   38.4
3    MS-0975   39.3
4    MS-0297   38.0
5    MS-0159   38.9

# b)
mean(measles$temp_c[measles$outcome == "Died"])

[1] 38.754

# c)
nrow(measles[measles$age_years >= 15, ])

[1] 225

nrow(filter(measles, age_years >= 15))

[1] 196

nrow(measles[measles$age_years >= 15 & !is.na(measles$age_years), ])   # fixed

[1] 196


Base R gives 225 rows because it adds a row of NAs for each of the 29 cases with a missing age. Adding & !is.na(measles$age_years) gives 196, the same as filter().











Note📖 Good to know




Where you’ll meet base R: help-page examples (?mean), answers on Stack Overflow, older scripts, and many Bioconductor packages. Being able to read it is the main skill; you can keep writing tidyverse code.
Out-of-range positions don’t give an error: temps_c[10] gives NA, because there is no tenth value. If you see unexpected NAs after subsetting, check your positions.

Pulling things out

patient$symptoms     # $ with a name you type

[1] "fever" "cough"

patient[["age"]]     # [[ ]] with a name in quotes (or a position)

[1] 2

patient["age"]       # [ ] gives back a smaller LIST, not the value

$age
[1] 2

length(patient)      # 4 elements

[1] 4

str(patient)         # the structure: what is in each element

List of 4
 $ id      : chr "5fe599"
 $ age     : num 2
 $ symptoms: chr [1:2] "fever" "cough"
 $ visits  : Date[1:2], format: "2014-05-13" "2014-05-15"








Note🔍 What this code does




list() stores four different things together, each with a name: a piece of text, a number, two symptoms, and two dates.
patient$symptoms and patient[["age"]] take one element out: the vector itself.
patient["age"] gives back a list with one element in it. The output shows the difference: it starts with $age. You can’t calculate with it: patient["age"] + 1 gives an error.
length(patient) counts the elements: 4. str() shows one line per element with its type and size: chr, num, chr [1:2], and Date[1:2].



Think of a list as a box of items: [[ ]] takes an item out of the box; [ ] gives you a smaller box.

section: A data frame is a list
text:
A data frame is a list
A data frame is a list of columns that all have the same length. You saw one drawn as boxes in Session 1; now build it yourself:

👀 Follow along 5.2 — Build the small patients data frame with data.frame() and pull out one column with $. Then is.list(linelist) and length(linelist): a data frame is a list!
Pattern: data.frame(COLUMN_1 = c(...), COLUMN_2 = c(...))


patients <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cho"),
  age  = c(34, 51, 27)
)
patients

  name age
1  Ana  34
2  Ben  51
3  Cho  27

patients$age         # $ pulls out one column

[1] 34 51 27

is.list(linelist)

[1] TRUE

length(linelist)     # the number of columns

[1] 19








Note🔍 What this code does




data.frame() builds a table from vectors. Each column_name = c(...) becomes one column: name holds text and age holds numbers. Every column must have the same length (3 here), because each row is one patient.
patients$age pulls out the age column as a vector: 34 51 27, the same way $ takes an element out of a list.
is.list(linelist) is TRUE: a data frame is a list whose elements are its columns.
So length(linelist) counts the columns, 19, not the rows. Use nrow() for the number of rows.



That is why $ and [[ ]] work on data frames too, and why map() in Session 8 runs once for each column.

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Lists, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
Results are lists
Statistical tests and models return lists. You don’t need to know the statistics yet; look at the shape of the result (reading only, you don’t need to type this; you can try it yourself in the ⭐ Bonus):

age_test <- t.test(age_years ~ gender, data = filter(linelist, gender != "Unknown"))
age_test


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  age_years by gender
t = -21.98, df = 5390.7, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group female and group male is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -7.441575 -6.222858
sample estimates:
mean in group female   mean in group male 
            12.68343             19.51564 


The printout is a friendly view for people. Underneath, it is a list your code can use:

names(age_test)

 [1] "statistic"   "parameter"   "p.value"     "conf.int"    "estimate"   
 [6] "null.value"  "stderr"      "alternative" "method"      "data.name"  

age_test$p.value

[1] 1.271186e-102

age_test$estimate

mean in group female   mean in group male 
            12.68343             19.51564 








Note🔍 What this code does




t.test(age_years ~ gender, ...) compares the mean age of the two genders. Read ~ as “by”: age by gender.
data = filter(linelist, gender != "Unknown") gives t.test() only the rows with a known gender, because it needs exactly two groups.
age_test is a list. names(age_test) lists its 10 elements, such as p.value, estimate, and conf.int.
age_test$p.value takes out the p-value as a plain number: 1.271186e-102, R’s way of writing 1.27 × 10-102 (extremely small). age_test$estimate gives the two means: 12.7 years (female) and 19.5 years (male).



Every test and model in R works this way (chisq.test(), lm(), glm(), survival models, Bioconductor objects), so this is how you get one number out of an analysis and into a table or a report.






WarningCommon mistakes




patient["age"] + 1 gives an error: [ ] returns a list. Use patient[["age"]] or patient$age.
t.test() compares exactly two groups. “grouping factor must have exactly 2 levels” means there is a third group (like “Unknown”): filter() it out first.









Note📖 Good to know




When you get an object you don’t recognize (from a test, a model, or someone else’s code), try str() and names() first. They show what’s inside and what you can pull out with $.
The broom package (installed with the tidyverse) turns test and model results into data frames: broom::tidy(age_test) gives a one-row table with the means and the p-value, ready for a report.

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Lists, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
Tidy data
Data is tidy when:

Each variable is a column
Each observation is a row
Each value is a cell

The tidyverse works best on tidy data. But “observation” depends on your question. Our symptoms are in wide format — one column per symptom:

👀 Follow along 6.1 — Look at the symptom columns: linelist %>% select(case_id, fever:vomit).


linelist %>% select(case_id, fever:vomit) %>% head(3)

  case_id   fever  chills   cough   aches   vomit
1  5fe599      no      no     yes      no     yes
2  8689b7 Unknown Unknown Unknown Unknown Unknown
3  11f8ea Unknown Unknown Unknown Unknown Unknown








Note🔍 What this code does




select(case_id, fever:vomit) keeps the ID and the five symptom columns: fever, chills, cough, aches, and vomit. head(3) shows the first 3 patients.
Each symptom has its own column, with “yes”, “no”, or “Unknown” in each cell. This is wide format.



To count or plot all symptoms together, we want long format: one row per patient per symptom. Here are the first two patients and two of their symptoms, before and after:

  
    Wide: one row per patient
    case_idfevercough
    5fe599noyes
    8689b7UnknownUnknown
  
  ↓ pivot_longer()
  
    Long: one row per patient per symptom
    case_idsymptompresent
    5fe599feverno
    5fe599coughyes
    8689b7feverUnknown
    8689b7coughUnknown
  

The orange boxes are the old column names: they become values in the new symptom column. The blue boxes are the old cells: they move into the new present column. case_id is repeated once for each symptom.

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Lists, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
pivot_longer(): wide → long

👀 Follow along 6.2 — pivot_longer() the five symptoms into symptoms_long, and check nrow().


symptoms_long <- linelist %>%
  select(case_id, fever:vomit) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = fever:vomit,   # the columns to stack
    names_to  = "symptom",     # new column for the old column NAMES
    values_to = "present"      # new column for the VALUES
  )

head(symptoms_long)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  case_id symptom present
  <chr>   <chr>   <chr>  
1 5fe599  fever   no     
2 5fe599  chills  no     
3 5fe599  cough   yes    
4 5fe599  aches   no     
5 5fe599  vomit   yes    
6 8689b7  fever   Unknown

nrow(symptoms_long)   # 6451 patients × 5 symptoms

[1] 32255


fever:vomit means “every column from fever to vomit”.






Tip🧩 Reading a function call



Here is the key call of this session, taken apart:
pivot_longer(cols = fever:vomit, names_to = "symptom", values_to = "present")








Piece
What it is
What it does




pivot_longer(...)
a function from the tidyr package (part of the tidyverse)
reshapes wide data into long data


the data
arrives through the pipe %>% as the first argument, so you don’t type it
the table to reshape


cols = fever:vomit
an argument: which columns to stack
the five columns from fever to vomit


names_to = "symptom"
an argument: the name of a new column, in quotes
will hold the old column names (fever, chills, …)


values_to = "present"
an argument: the name of another new column
will hold the values from the old cells (yes, no, Unknown)



Because every argument is named, you can read the call like a sentence: “pivot longer the columns fever to vomit; put their names into symptom and their values into present.” The new column names are in quotes because those columns don’t exist yet. fever:vomit isn’t, because those columns already exist.








Note🔍 What this code does




select() keeps the ID and the five symptoms, as before.
pivot_longer() stacks the five symptom columns, so each patient now has five rows, one per symptom.
The old column names (fever, chills, …) go into the new symptom column, and the yes/no values go into the new present column.
case_id isn’t in cols, so it’s repeated on each of the patient’s five rows.
nrow() confirms the size: 6451 patients × 5 symptoms = 32255 rows.



Now one count() answers “how many patients had each symptom?”:

👀 Follow along 6.3 — Count the patients with each symptom: filter() present == "yes", then count().


symptom_counts <- symptoms_long %>%
  filter(present == "yes") %>%
  count(symptom)

symptom_counts

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  symptom     n
  <chr>   <int>
1 aches     604
2 chills   1209
3 cough    5347
4 fever    5077
5 vomit    3095


And it’s ready to plot. This is a preview of Session 6, so it’s reading only:

ggplot(symptom_counts, aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(symptom, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Patients reporting each symptom", x = "Number of patients", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()














Note🔍 What this code does




filter(present == "yes") keeps only the rows where the patient had that symptom.
count(symptom) counts the rows left for each symptom: cough 5347, fever 5077, vomit 3095, chills 1209, and aches 604.
Because the data is long, one count() does what would take five separate counts in the wide data.
ggplot() draws one bar per symptom: geom_col() uses n as the bar length, and fct_reorder(symptom, n) orders the bars by length, so the longest is at the top. You’ll learn plotting in Session 6.









Important✏️ TRY IT 5 (5 min): measles symptoms long



Select patient_id, fever, and rash from measles, then pivot_longer() the two symptom columns. count() symptom and present.
Pattern: pivot_longer(cols = c(COLUMN_1, COLUMN_2), names_to = "symptom", values_to = "present")
✅ Check: 2326 rows (1163 × 2); fever yes 1064, rash yes 976






NoteShow solution






measles_symptoms <- measles %>%
  select(patient_id, fever, rash) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(fever, rash),
    names_to  = "symptom",
    values_to = "present"
  )

nrow(measles_symptoms)

[1] 2326

measles_symptoms %>% count(symptom, present)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  symptom present     n
  <chr>   <chr>   <int>
1 fever   no         99
2 fever   yes      1064
3 rash    no        187
4 rash    yes       976


Each of the 1163 cases now has two rows, one for fever and one for rash, so there are 2326 rows. One count() gives the yes/no totals for both symptoms.











Note📖 Good to know




How to tell wide from long: if some column names are really values of a variable (fever, chills, cough, or years like 2019, 2020, 2021), the data is wide. Spreadsheets are usually wide; count(), ggplot(), and most tidyverse functions work best on long data.

text:

Where this session fits. Today is about one step, Visualize (highlighted): turning the clean data into plots that show its patterns. Session 7 continues with more kinds of plots and with saving them to files.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Fixed colors
Inside geom_histogram(), fill is the inside color and color is the outline. A white outline separates the bars.

👀 Follow along 3.2 — Add fill = "#2a78d6" and color = "white".


ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")














Note🔍 What this code does




fill and color are given inside geom_histogram(), so they apply to every bar. fill colors the inside of the bars, and color the outline.
"#2a78d6" is a hex code for a blue: a #, then two characters each for the amount of red, green, and blue.
The white outline draws a thin line between neighboring bars, so you can tell them apart.









NoteColors in R



Use a name ("steelblue", "gray50") or a hex code ("#2a78d6"). Run colors() to see all 657 named colors.








Important✏️ TRY IT 3 (3 min): measles ages



Make a histogram of measles age_years with binwidth = 1, a fill color, and a white outline. Which age has the most cases?
✅ Check: the tallest bar is at age 2 (about 100 cases). The warning about “removed rows” is the 29 missing ages: that’s fine.






NoteShow solution






ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")








The tallest bar is age 2 (102 cases), and most cases are ages 1–5. ggplot can’t draw the 29 rows with a missing age, so it drops them and tells you.











Note📖 Good to know




A histogram is for one number, like age: the bars touch because the ranges follow each other. For categories, like hospital or outcome, you use a bar chart instead (Session 7).
When ggplot can’t draw some rows, because a value is missing, it drops them and tells you how many in a warning. Read the number: it’s a quick check that it’s the count of missing values you expected.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
section: Map a third variable to color
text:
Map a third variable to color

ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg, color = gender)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.4)














Note🔍 What this code does




size = 1 makes the points smaller, and alpha = 0.3 makes them 70% see-through. Where many points overlap, the color builds up and looks darker, so you can see where most patients are.
These are settings, so they go in geom_point(), outside aes().
In the second plot, color = gender is inside aes(): a mapping. Each gender gets its own color and a legend entry. Points use color; bars and boxes use fill for the inside.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Add a trend line
geom_smooth() adds a trend line on top of the points. method = "lm" draws a straight line (linear model); se = FALSE hides the confidence band.

👀 Follow along 5.3 — Add geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#eb6834").


ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#eb6834")














Note🔍 What this code does




geom_smooth() adds a second layer on top of the points. Both layers use the same aes() from ggplot(), so the line uses the same x and y.
method = "lm" draws the straight line that fits the points best (a linear model). se = FALSE hides the gray band that shows how uncertain the line is.
The line starts at about 34 kg at age 0 and rises about 1.2 kg per year of age. A straight line can’t bend, so it misses how fast children grow.
The message “geom_smooth() using formula = ‘y ~ x’” just tells you what the line fits: y (weight) from x (age).

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Filter right inside ggplot()
You can pipe data into ggplot(), so you can filter() first without making a new object:

👀 Follow along 5.4 — Only patients with fever: filter() first, then ggplot().


linelist %>%
  filter(fever == "yes") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.3)














Note🔍 What this code does




linelist %>% filter(fever == "yes") keeps the 5077 patients with fever. The pipe then passes them into ggplot() as its data.
There’s no data = in ggplot(), because the pipe already supplies the data.
After ggplot(), layers are joined with +. The rule: %>% before ggplot(), + after it.
linelist itself isn’t changed: the filter only applies to this plot.



Notice the switch: %>% into ggplot(), then + between layers.






Important✏️ TRY IT 5 (4 min): a scatter plot



For hospitalized patients only (filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital))), plot age_years (x) against days_in_hospital (y) with alpha, and add a trend line. Is there a relationship?
✅ Check: 427 hospitalized patients; the trend line is almost flat (no relationship)






NoteShow solution






measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = days_in_hospital)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#eb6834")








The trend line is almost flat: older and younger patients stay in hospital about as long. “No relationship” is a result too!











Note📖 Good to know




Each geometry has its own aesthetics. Points use color, size, shape, and alpha; bars and boxes use fill for the inside and color for the outline. The help page (for example ?geom_point) lists them under Aesthetics.
A trend line shows a pattern, not a cause. Here, weight rises with age because children grow, not because of the outbreak.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Clean it up
Remove the “Unknown” group, color the boxes, and drop the legend (the x-axis already names the groups):

👀 Follow along 6.2 — Filter out “Unknown”, add fill = gender, and remove the legend.


linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")














Note🔍 What this code does




filter(gender != "Unknown") keeps every row where gender is not “Unknown”. != means “not equal”.
fill = gender inside aes() colors each box by gender.
theme(legend.position = "none") removes the legend. The x-axis already names each box, so a legend would only repeat it.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Add the mean
stat_summary() calculates a statistic for each group and draws it. Here, the mean as a diamond:

👀 Follow along 6.3 — Add the mean with stat_summary().


linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")














Note🔍 What this code does




stat_summary() calculates one number for each group and draws it. fun = mean calculates the mean age, and geom = "point" draws it as a point.
shape = 23 is a diamond that can be filled, size = 3 makes it bigger, and fill = "white" makes it white so it stands out against the box.
The means are 12.7 years (female) and 19.5 (male).









Note🤔 Think about it: why is the mean (diamond) above the median (line)?





The ages are right-skewed: a few older patients pull the mean up. For example, the median age of female cases is 11 but the mean is 12.7.









Note



geom_violin() shows the full shape of each distribution. Try swapping it in for geom_boxplot().








Important✏️ TRY IT 6 (4 min): a box plot



Make a box plot of days_in_hospital by vaccinated (hospitalized patients only), with the mean and no legend.
✅ Check: three boxes; the medians are 4–5 days for every group






NoteShow solution






measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = vaccinated, y = days_in_hospital, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








The medians are 4 days (Yes) and 5 days (No, Unknown), and the means are all about 5: no clear difference in hospital stay by vaccination status. The boxes appear in the order you set with fct_relevel() in Part 1.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
labs()

👀 Follow along 7.1 — Add labs() to the box plot.


linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title    = "Age distribution by gender",
    subtitle = "Cases with known gender",
    x        = "Gender",
    y        = "Age (years)",
    caption  = "Source: workshop outbreak linelist"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")














Note🔍 What this code does




labs() sets the text around the plot: the title, a subtitle, the x and y axis labels, and a caption at the bottom, often used for the data source.
Each label is text, so it’s in quotes. Lining up the = signs is optional: it only makes the code easier to read.
labs() is one more layer, added with +. The data and the boxes stay the same.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Themes
A theme changes the look of everything that isn’t data: background, grid lines, fonts. Try theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), theme_bw(), and theme_light().

👀 Follow along 7.2 — Try theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), and theme_bw() on the age histogram.


ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution of cases",
    x     = "Age (years)",
    y     = "Number of cases"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)














Note🔍 What this code does




theme_minimal() is a complete theme: it restyles everything that isn’t data. Here it removes the gray background.
base_size = 14 sets the size of all the text at once (the default is 11).
Swap in theme_classic() or theme_bw() to compare: only the look changes, never the data.



base_size makes all the text bigger — useful for slides.






WarningOrder matters



A complete theme like theme_minimal() resets everything, so put it before theme(legend.position = ...) or your change will be overwritten.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
section: Save a plot as an object
text:
Save a plot as an object
A plot can be saved with <- and built on later:

👀 Follow along 7.3 — Save a plot as age_plot, then add labs() and a theme to it.


age_plot <- ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")

age_plot +
  labs(title = "Age distribution of cases", x = "Age (years)", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_minimal()














Note🔍 What this code does




age_plot <- ggplot(...) + geom_histogram(...) saves the plot as an object instead of drawing it. age_plot appears in the Variables pane.
age_plot + labs(...) + theme_minimal() adds layers to the saved plot and draws the result. age_plot itself doesn’t change unless you save again with <-.
This way you can try different labels and themes without retyping the whole plot.









Important✏️ TRY IT 7 (5 min): finish a plot



Finish one of your measles plots with a title, subtitle, axis labels, a caption, and a theme. Save it as my_plot.
✅ Check: typing my_plot in the Console shows your finished plot






NoteShow solution






my_plot <- ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = temp_c, fill = fever)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, color = "white") +
  labs(
    title    = "Temperature of measles cases",
    subtitle = "Patients with fever cluster around 39 °C",
    x        = "Temperature (°C)",
    y        = "Number of cases",
    fill     = "Fever",
    caption  = "Source: practice measles linelist"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

my_plot








This is one example — any measles plot works. fill = "Fever" inside labs() renames the legend title. Saving the plot as my_plot stores it in the Variables pane, and typing its name draws it.











Note📖 Good to know: which plot for which question?











Your question
Plot
Geometry




How is one number spread out?
Histogram
geom_histogram()


Are two numbers related?
Scatter plot
geom_point()


Does a number differ between groups?
Box plot
geom_boxplot()


How many in each category?
Bar chart (Session 7)
geom_bar()


How do cases change over time?
Epidemic curve (Session 7)
geom_histogram() with dates



To save a plot as an image file, use ggsave(): that’s in Session 7.








Tip⭐ Bonus




Make the measles age histogram with fill = vaccinated. Which ages have the most unvaccinated cases?
Swap geom_boxplot() for geom_violin() in your box plot. What does it show?
Brought your own data? Make a histogram, a scatter plot, and a box plot.

See the solutions file for the code.

text:
⬇ Student script ⬇ Solutions ⬇ Workshop folder (ZIP)
Where this session fits. Most data projects go through the same steps, whatever the topic. This session covers the last one, Automate (highlighted): turning steps you repeat into functions and loops, so one line of code redoes the whole job, for example next week’s epidemic curves.

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
text:
Why write functions?
If you copy and paste code more than twice, write a function. Functions:

avoid copy-paste mistakes (change it once, fixed everywhere)
give a task a clear name (c_to_f() says what it does)
make your scripts shorter and easier to read
crumbs: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
text:
The shape of a function

👀 Follow along 2.1 — Write c_to_f(temp_c) and test it on 38 and on c(36.8, 38.5, 40.1) (the next two code blocks).


c_to_f <- function(temp_c) {
  temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32
}


c_to_f is the name — you save a function with <- like any object. Run the whole block to create it; then it appears in the Variables pane
temp_c is the argument — the input. Inside the function, it is whatever value you pass in
The code between { } is the body
The function returns the result of its last line


c_to_f(38)

[1] 100.4

c_to_f(c(36.8, 38.5, 40.1))   # it's vectorized, because the maths inside is

[1]  98.24 101.30 104.18








Note🔍 What this code does




c_to_f(38) runs the body with temp_c set to 38: 38 × 9 / 5 + 32 = 100.4.
c_to_f(c(36.8, 38.5, 40.1)) converts all three at once: 98.24, 101.3, and 104.18. You didn’t write a loop: *, /, and + already work on every value in a vector, so your function does too.
temp_c only exists while the function runs. It doesn’t appear in the Variables pane.



Because it’s vectorized, it works on a whole column inside mutate():

👀 Follow along 2.2 — Use c_to_f() inside mutate() to add temp_f to linelist.


linelist %>%
  mutate(temp_f = c_to_f(temp)) %>%
  select(case_id, temp, temp_f) %>%
  head(3)

  case_id temp temp_f
1  5fe599 36.8  98.24
2  8689b7 36.9  98.42
3  11f8ea 36.9  98.42








Note🔍 What this code does




mutate(temp_f = c_to_f(temp)) gives the whole temp column to c_to_f() and stores the answers in a new column, temp_f. 36.8 °C becomes 98.24 °F.
select() and head(3) just keep the output short. linelist itself doesn’t change, because the result isn’t saved with <-.
crumbs: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
text:
Default values
Give an argument a default with =. You can change it, but you don’t have to:

👀 Follow along 2.3 — Add a digits = 1 default argument with round().


c_to_f <- function(temp_c, digits = 1) {
  round(temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32, digits)
}

c_to_f(38.37)              # uses digits = 1

[1] 101.1

c_to_f(38.37, digits = 0)  # overrides it

[1] 101








Note🔍 What this code does




This new c_to_f() replaces the old one, because it’s saved under the same name.
digits = 1 inside function() sets a default. c_to_f(38.37) doesn’t mention digits, so it uses 1 and gives 101.1.
c_to_f(38.37, digits = 0) overrides the default and rounds to a whole number: 101.
Inside the body, round(..., digits) passes your choice on to round().









WarningCommon mistakes




Changing the function but not re-running the block: R still uses the old version.









Important✏️ TRY IT 2 (4 min): Fahrenheit to Celsius



Write f_to_c(temp_f) that converts Fahrenheit to Celsius: (temp_f - 32) * 5 / 9, rounded to 1 decimal. Test it on 98.6 and 104.7.
✅ Check: f_to_c(98.6) is 37 and f_to_c(104.7) is 40.4






NoteShow solution






f_to_c <- function(temp_f) {
  round((temp_f - 32) * 5 / 9, 1)
}

f_to_c(98.6)

[1] 37

f_to_c(104.7)

[1] 40.4


104.7 °F is 40.4 °C — the Fahrenheit temperature you found in the measles data in Session 1!











Note📖 Good to know




Functions you write live in R’s memory, like any object. They’re gone when R restarts, so keep them in your script, near the top, and run them before you use them.
Give functions names that say what they do, such as make_epicurve() or c_to_f(). Avoid names that R already uses, like mean or c: your version would hide the original.
In other people’s code you may see return(x). It ends the function and gives back x. Without it, the function returns its last line. Both are fine.

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
section: A calculation used in many places
text:
A calculation used in many places

👀 Follow along 3.1 — Write pct(x, digits = 1), which returns round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, digits), and use it in summarise() by hospital.


pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, digits)
}

linelist %>%
  group_by(hospital_name) %>%
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    pct_death = pct(outcome == "Death"),
    pct_fever = pct(fever == "yes")
  )

# A tibble: 7 × 4
  hospital_name                     n pct_death pct_fever
  <chr>                         <int>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Central Hospital                454      42.5      77.3
2 HMO Health                      280      44.3      92.9
3 Military Hospital               896      44.5      79  
4 Other/Unknown                  2354      42.7      77.3
5 Premiere Health                 274      47.1      94.5
6 Regional Medical center        1771      44.6      76.7
7 St. Mark's Maternity Hospital   422      47.2      75.8


Compare with Session 5, where we wrote round(mean(...) * 100, 1) every time.






Note🔍 What this code does




pct() expects a vector of TRUE and FALSE. The mean() of TRUE/FALSE values is the share that are TRUE (TRUE counts as 1, FALSE as 0). * 100 makes it a percentage, and na.rm = TRUE skips missing values.
outcome == "Death" is TRUE for every patient who died, so pct(outcome == "Death") is the percentage who died: 44.5% at Military Hospital.
group_by(hospital_name) makes summarise() do this once per hospital, giving 7 rows (including Other/Unknown).

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
section: A function that takes a data frame
text:
A function that takes a data frame

👀 Follow along 3.2 — Write hospital_summary(data, hospital) and try it on two hospitals.


hospital_summary <- function(data, hospital) {
  data %>%
    filter(hospital_name == hospital) %>%
    summarise(
      n         = n(),
      pct_death = pct(outcome == "Death")
    )
}

hospital_summary(linelist, "Military Hospital")

    n pct_death
1 896      44.5

hospital_summary(linelist, "Central Hospital")

    n pct_death
1 454      42.5


hospital is an argument holding a value (the hospital’s name), so it can go straight into filter().






Note🔍 What this code does




hospital_summary() takes two arguments: the data, and the name of one hospital.
Inside, filter(hospital_name == hospital) keeps that hospital’s rows. summarise() then counts them and works out the death percentage with your own pct() function. A function can use other functions you wrote, as long as you’ve run them first.
Same function, different input: Military Hospital has 896 cases (44.5% died) and Central Hospital has 454 (42.5%).

section: A function that makes a plot
text:
A function that makes a plot

👀 Follow along 3.3 — Write make_epicurve(data, hospital), which returns a weekly epicurve for one hospital, with the hospital’s name in the title.


make_epicurve <- function(data, hospital) {
  data %>%
    filter(hospital_name == hospital, onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = onset_date)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Weekly cases:", hospital),
      x     = "Week of onset",
      y     = "Number of cases"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

make_epicurve(linelist, "Military Hospital")








paste("Weekly cases:", hospital) builds the title from the argument, so every plot gets the right title.






Note🔍 What this code does




The body is an ordinary plot pipeline. filter() keeps one hospital, and geom_histogram(binwidth = 7) puts each week’s cases into one bar.
onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01") also drops onset dates before 2014, which would stretch the time axis back to 2012.
A function returns its last value, and here that’s the plot, so make_epicurve(linelist, "Military Hospital") draws it. You could also save it first: p <- make_epicurve(linelist, "Military Hospital").









WarningCommon mistake: name the argument district_name, not district



Don’t give an argument the same name as a column! In
function(data, district) { data %>% filter(district == district) }
R compares the district column with itself, so every row is kept — no error, just the wrong answer. Name the argument district_name instead: filter(district == district_name).








Important✏️ TRY IT 3 (6 min): measles functions




Write rate_per_10k(cases, population) that returns cases / population * 10000, rounded to 1 decimal. Use it in mutate() after count(district, population).
Write district_summary(data, district_name) that returns the number of cases and the percentage vaccinated (use your pct() function!) for one district.

✅ Check: a) East is 22.8 b) district_summary(measles, "North") gives n 342, 25.7%






NoteShow solution






# a)
rate_per_10k <- function(cases, population) {
  round(cases / population * 10000, 1)
}

measles %>%
  count(district, population) %>%
  mutate(rate = rate_per_10k(n, population)) %>%
  arrange(desc(rate))

  district population   n rate
1     East      98000 223 22.8
2     West      76500 170 22.2
3    South     142000 284 20.0
4    North     185000 342 18.5
5  Central     210000 110  5.2
6  Unknown         NA  34   NA

# b)
district_summary <- function(data, district_name) {
  data %>%
    filter(district == district_name) %>%
    summarise(
      n              = n(),
      pct_vaccinated = pct(vaccinated == "Yes")
    )
}

district_summary(measles, "North")

    n pct_vaccinated
1 342           25.7


East has the highest rate, 22.8 cases per 10,000. North has 342 cases, and 25.7% of them were vaccinated. Because the argument is called district_name, filter(district == district_name) keeps only North.
